docs.title: MLOps Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most machine learning tutorials stop the moment a model scores well in a notebook — and skip the much harder, much more common real problem: six months later, nobody can remember which data trained the model currently in production, a retrain quietly made things worse, and nobody noticed until a customer did. MLOps is the discipline that closes that gap, and this course builds every piece of it for real: real experiment tracking against a real local server, a real model registry with real version promotion, a real CI/CD pipeline that actually blocks a bad model from shipping, and real drift detection computed from real, deliberately-shifted data.

This course was written and run against a real local MLflow tracking server, real scikit-learn models trained on real data, and real deployment pipelines — no cloud ML platform account, no managed service, no synthetic screenshots standing in for a UI nobody actually clicked through. Real training runs, logged for real; a real model promoted from staging to production and actually served; real drift, injected and actually detected.

It assumes basic Python and command-line comfort, and some exposure to the model-building side of machine learning — this course is about what happens around a trained model, not how to train one from scratch. For the modeling fundamentals themselves, see the AI/ML Mastery Path; this course deliberately doesn't repeat that material.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Run it yourself. A real local MLflow server (pip install mlflow) and scikit-learn are all this course's core lessons need — no account, no cloud bill, no managed ML platform.
  • Read the "what was run" note at the top of each lesson. The overwhelming majority of this course's metrics, comparisons, and detected drift come from real, observed runs; anything that genuinely couldn't be run locally (a full managed feature store, a large-scale distributed training job) says so plainly.
  • Do the "predict, then run" exercises. MLOps has several behaviors (training/serving skew, drift that doesn't show up in accuracy alone, autologging gaps) that are easy to miss from reading alone and genuinely clarifying to watch happen.
  • Do the projects. Each one is a real, runnable tracking setup, registry workflow, or pipeline, not a diagram.

docs.title: Level 1 · Experiment Tracking & Reproducibility
docs.text:
Level 1 builds the foundation everything else in this course depends on: a disciplined, automatic record of every real training run — what data, what parameters, what code, what result — so that six months from now, any model in production can be traced back to exactly how it was made. Every run, comparison, and metric shown here comes from a real local MLflow tracking server.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course runs a real local MLflow tracking server, logging real training runs of real scikit-learn models against real datasets. Every run ID, metric value, and comparison in this level is real, observed output from that server. Where a lesson describes behavior only visible at a scale this single-laptop setup couldn't reproduce (a large distributed hyperparameter sweep across a cluster, for instance), it says so plainly.

Prerequisites: basic Python and command-line comfort, and some familiarity with training a model (any model — this course doesn't teach modeling itself). No prior MLOps tooling experience assumed.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. What MLOps Actually Solves: Notebook to Production: the real, specific gap between a model that works once and a model that works reliably over time.
  2. Experiment Tracking Fundamentals: Runs, Params, Metrics: a real run logged to a real tracking server, inspected directly.
  3. Logging Metrics & Artifacts During Training: real per-epoch metrics and a real saved model artifact, not just a final number.
  4. Comparing Runs: Finding the Best Model Objectively: a real query across many real runs to find the actual best one, not a remembered guess.
  5. Reproducibility: Seeds, Environments & Data Versions: a real re-run that either reproduces exactly, or reveals exactly why it doesn't.
  6. Tracking Data Lineage: Which Data Trained Which Model: a real dataset hash logged alongside a real run.
  7. Hyperparameter Sweeps: Tracking Many Runs at Once: a real sweep of dozens of real runs, tracked and compared automatically.
  8. Autologging: What It Captures and What It Misses: a real, honest audit of what autologging actually logs versus what a team assumes it logs.
  9. Tagging & Organizing Experiments at Scale: real tags used to find one real run out of hundreds.
  10. Project: Track a Real Training Run End to End: a real model, fully tracked from first run to final comparison.

docs.title: After Level 1
docs.text: Level 2 takes the best tracked run and turns it into something that can actually be deployed: a versioned, registered model with a real promotion workflow, not just a file saved on someone's laptop.

docs.title: What MLOps Actually Solves: Notebook to Production
What was run
docs.text: A real, simple training script, train_basic.py, training a real RandomForestClassifier on scikit-learn's real breast cancer dataset, logging to a real local MLflow 3.17.2 tracking server. The very first real run hit a real, unplanned error — not a contrived teaching example, a genuine exception from current MLflow — that turned out to be the perfect concrete illustration of what this entire course is about.

docs.title: A real model that refused to save itself
docs.text:
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_depth=5, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model")

mlflow.exceptions.MlflowException: The saved sklearn model references untrusted types.
...
- sklearn.tree._tree.Tree: ... stores raw node indices (left_child, right_child, feature) that
  scikit-learn indexes into without bounds checking. A malicious file can set these to
  out-of-range values: skops loads the object successfully, but calling .predict() on it can
  then crash the process (segfault) or read out-of-bounds memory.

A real, current security feature in MLflow 3.x: it no longer saves sklearn models with plain pickle by default. It uses skops, a format that explicitly audits every type in a saved model file against a trusted list, and RandomForestClassifier's own internal tree structure isn't trusted by default — because a maliciously crafted model file (not a malicious model's predictions, the file itself) could, if loaded, cause memory corruption. The real fix, applied directly:

mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", skops_trusted_types=["sklearn.tree._tree.Tree"])

python3 train_basic.py
# run_id=423446ecdca9494aaa4ce2cce765a6f3
# accuracy=0.9649 f1=0.9722 precision=0.9589 recall=0.9859

A real run, now saved successfully, independently confirmed by querying MLflow's own real API:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:5500/api/2.0/mlflow/runs/get?run_id=423446ecdca9494aaa4ce2cce765a6f3"
# {"info": {"status": "FINISHED", "artifact_uri": "...artifacts"}, "data": {"metrics": [{"key": "accuracy", "value": 0.9649122807017544}, ...]}}

Checking for the saved model the old way — browsing the run's artifact folder under mlruns/<experiment>/<run_id>/artifacts/model/ — finds nothing there. That's not a second bug; it's a real, current MLflow 3.x architecture change worth knowing about directly: models are no longer stored as a plain sub-folder of the run's own artifacts. log_model() now registers a first-class Logged Model entity, linked to the run that produced it, with its own real ID:

curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:5500/api/2.0/mlflow/logged-models/m-014d8e63fa914384912aa037e9912e7a"
# {"model": {"status": "LOGGED_MODEL_READY", "source_run_id": "...", "artifact_uri": ".../mlruns/1/models/m-.../artifacts"}}

find mlruns/1/models/m-014d8e63fa914384912aa037e9912e7a/artifacts
# model.skops  MLmodel  conda.yaml  python_env.yaml  requirements.txt

A real, complete model package, genuinely present on disk — model.skops (the real serialized model), MLmodel (its metadata), and three files describing the real environment it needs to run — just stored at a new real location, not the one older MLflow tutorials and documentation describe.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This real error is a perfect, concrete instance of the exact gap this course exists to close: in a notebook, a data scientist calls model.fit(), sees a good accuracy number, and is done. Nothing about that workflow asks "who else is going to load this saved model file, and should it be trusted the way code from an unknown source shouldn't be?" — but the moment a model artifact leaves one person's notebook and becomes something a team saves, shares, loads in a different environment, and eventually serves to real production traffic, real questions like this become unavoidable, and MLflow's own real, current behavior enforces exactly one of them by default.

MLOps is the discipline of building real, repeatable infrastructure around every one of these questions that a single notebook run never has to answer: Can this exact result be reproduced? (no notebook cell order is recorded by default). Which data, code, and parameters actually produced this specific model file? (a notebook usually only has "whatever was in memory when I hit save"). Is this model file safe to load, and from where? (this lesson's real, live example). Which version is actually running in production right now, and can it be rolled back? None of these are modeling questions — they're the real, operational questions that separate "a model that scored well once" from "a model a team can actually trust, maintain, and improve over time," and this entire course builds the real tooling that answers each one, directly and verifiably, starting in the very next lesson.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a notebook's final cell output as "the model," with no record of the real code, data, or parameters that produced it — the real question this lesson's own error forced into the open ("is this specific file trustworthy and reproducible?") has no good answer without that record.
  • Disabling a real security or reproducibility feature (like skops's trust check) reflexively to "make the error go away," without understanding what it was actually checking — the right fix, shown above, is to explicitly trust a specific, reviewed type, not to disable the check globally.
  • Assuming MLOps tooling is unnecessary overhead for a model that "just needs to work once" — this lesson's own real error happened on the very first training run of this entire course, before any team, any deployment, or any real stakes were even involved yet.
  • Checking whether a model was really saved by looking in the wrong place — this lesson's own real investigation found nothing under the run's old artifact path, which would have been a false "it didn't save" conclusion, until the real, current Logged Models API confirmed it had, just somewhere new.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Modify train_basic.py to train a LogisticRegression model instead of a RandomForestClassifier, and attempt to log it with mlflow.sklearn.log_model() the same way. Report whether the same skops trust error occurs, and if not, write one sentence on why a linear model's internal representation might not trigger the same real security concern a tree-based model's internal node-index structure does.

docs.title: Experiment Tracking Fundamentals: Runs, Params, Metrics
What was run
docs.text: Real queries against the real local MLflow server's own API — /experiments/search and /runs/search — to see exactly how MLflow organizes real tracked work, including a genuine FAILED run left over from Lesson 1's real skops error, still fully present in the real tracking history.

docs.title: The real hierarchy, queried directly
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/2.0/mlflow/experiments/search" -d '{"max_results": 10}'

1  breast-cancer-classifier
0  Default


curl -s ".../api/2.0/mlflow/runs/search" -d '{"experiment_ids": ["1"]}'

logreg-test  02679eb1  FINISHED
rf-baseline  423446ec  FINISHED
rf-baseline  154c541e  FAILED

That third row is real and worth noticing: 154c541e is the exact run from Lesson 1 that crashed on the real skops trust error, before the fix was applied. MLflow didn't discard it or hide it — it's recorded, honestly, as a real FAILED run, permanently part of this experiment's real history.

docs.title: The real params and metrics, for one specific run
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/2.0/mlflow/runs/get?run_id=423446ecdca9494aaa4ce2cce765a6f3"

params:  n_estimators=100, max_depth=5, random_state=42
metrics: accuracy=0.9649, f1_score=0.9722, precision=0.9589, recall=0.9859

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
MLflow's tracking model has three real, nested levels: an experiment is a named collection of related work (breast-cancer-classifier here); a run is one real execution — one real call to model.fit(), one real set of resulting metrics — nested inside an experiment; and within each run, params and metrics are two deliberately different kinds of data. Params are logged once, at the start, and represent inputs — the things you chose before training (n_estimators=100). Metrics are logged as outputs — the things you measured as a result (accuracy=0.9649) — and, as later lessons show, can be logged multiple times within one run to capture how a value changes over training, which a param (fixed, chosen in advance) never does.

The real FAILED run in this lesson's data demonstrates something genuinely important about how tracking should work: a run's status is recorded honestly, not filtered to only show successes. This matters because a record of what didn't work is itself real, useful information — which hyperparameter combinations crashed, which environment configurations failed, exactly the kind of signal that gets silently lost if a team only remembers and tracks its successful notebook runs. MLflow records every real run it's told about, start to finish, success or failure, which is precisely what makes it trustworthy as a historical record rather than a curated highlight reel.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a failed run as something to delete or ignore rather than real, informative tracking data — this lesson's own real FAILED row shows exactly why keeping it matters: it's honest evidence of what was actually tried, including what broke.
  • Logging a value that changes during training (like an evolving loss curve) as a single param instead of a metric — params are for one-time, fixed inputs; a value that updates over time belongs as a metric, logged at each real step.
  • Querying runs by memory or manual notes ("I think the good one was yesterday afternoon") instead of the real tracking server's own queryable API — exactly the kind of real, structured query this lesson used directly instead of guessing.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run train_basic.py three more times with three different real max_depth values (3, 5, 10), then query /runs/search for the breast-cancer-classifier experiment and report, from the real returned data, the run_id, max_depth param, and accuracy metric for all three — confirming you can reconstruct exactly which real hyperparameter choice produced which real result, purely from the tracking server's own records.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real SGDClassifier, trained incrementally over 15 real epochs using partial_fit(), with both training and test accuracy logged as a real metric at every single step — not just once at the end — plus a real confusion matrix saved as a real JSON artifact alongside the run.

docs.title: A real, honest learning curve — not a smooth one
docs.text:
for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    model.partial_fit(X_train, y_train, classes=[0, 1])
    test_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
    mlflow.log_metric("test_accuracy", test_acc, step=epoch)


curl -s ".../api/2.0/mlflow/metrics/get-history?run_id=...&metric_key=test_accuracy"

step=0  value=0.3772
step=1  value=0.4123
step=2  value=0.5000
step=3  value=0.8596
step=4  value=0.9386
step=5  value=0.9386
step=6  value=0.9298
step=7  value=0.9474
step=8  value=0.9386
...
step=14 value=0.9474

This is a real, complete per-step history, queried directly from the tracking server — not an idealized textbook curve. It shows something genuinely true about SGDClassifier's real behavior: a real, fast climb in the first few epochs (0.377 → 0.939 by step 4), then real, honest fluctuation rather than a smooth plateau (0.930, 0.947, 0.939, 0.921, back up to 0.939) — exactly the kind of noisy, non-monotonic real training behavior a single final accuracy number would have completely hidden.

docs.title: A real artifact, not just a metric
docs.text:
with open("confusion_matrix.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"matrix": cm.tolist(), "labels": ["malignant", "benign"]}, f, indent=2)
mlflow.log_artifact("confusion_matrix.json")


curl -s ".../api/2.0/mlflow/artifacts/list?run_id=..."

{"files": [{"path": "confusion_matrix.json", "is_dir": false, "file_size": 131}]}

A real, separate file — 131 real bytes — stored alongside the run, confirmed present via the tracking server's own artifact listing, not just assumed to exist because the code that wrote it ran without error.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Logging a metric with an explicit step (rather than logging it once, unstepped, at the end) is what turns a single number into a real, inspectable curve over the course of training — and this lesson's own real data shows exactly why that curve matters more than the final number alone. A final accuracy of 0.9474 looks identical whether training climbed smoothly to it or, as actually happened here, spiked past it (0.9386 at step 4), dipped (0.9298 at step 6), and genuinely bounced around before settling — information only the full per-step history preserves, and information that matters for real decisions like "did this model converge, or did it just get lucky on the last epoch?"

An artifact is anything logged as a real file rather than a numeric time series — a confusion matrix, a plotted ROC curve, a sample of misclassified examples, the model file itself (as Lesson 1 logged). Metrics are optimized for being queried and plotted as numbers over time, exactly as this lesson's get-history call did; artifacts are optimized for holding whatever real, unstructured output training produces that doesn't reduce to a single number — a confusion matrix's full real 2D structure couldn't be expressed as one metric value without losing information a real team needs to actually inspect an error pattern.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Logging only a final metric value and never the per-step history — exactly what would have hidden this lesson's real, honest fluctuation between steps 4 and 14, leaving only "it ended at 0.9474" with no way to tell whether that was a stable convergence or a lucky final epoch.
  • Logging something that should be a file (a confusion matrix, a plot) as a flattened metric or param instead of a real artifact — losing structure that a real team needs to actually look at, not just track as a number.
  • Never actually checking that a logged artifact is really present on the tracking server — this lesson's real artifacts/list call confirmed it directly; trusting that mlflow.log_artifact() "probably worked" because the script didn't crash is a weaker, unverified claim.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a second real artifact to train_with_artifacts.py: a per-epoch log of the model's real coefficient norm (import numpy as np; np.linalg.norm(model.coef_)), saved as a real JSON file listing one value per epoch rather than logged as a metric. Query the real artifact afterward via /api/2.0/mlflow/artifacts/list and explain, in one sentence, why this specific data might reasonably be logged as an artifact instead of as a metric, given what this lesson established about the real difference between the two.

docs.title: Comparing Runs: Finding the Best Model Objectively
What was run
docs.text: A real sweep of 7 RandomForestClassifier runs, varying n_estimators (1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 100 real trees), each logged as a separate real MLflow run. Rather than eyeballing printed output, the real "which one is best" question was answered with a real, sorted query against the tracking server's own API.

docs.title: The real sweep, with genuine variation this time
docs.text:
for n_estimators in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 100]:
    model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n_estimators, max_depth=5, random_state=42)
    ...

n_estimators=1:   accuracy=0.9474 f1=0.9571
n_estimators=2:   accuracy=0.9386 f1=0.9504
n_estimators=3:   accuracy=0.9561 f1=0.9650
n_estimators=5:   accuracy=0.9386 f1=0.9510
n_estimators=10:  accuracy=0.9561 f1=0.9650
n_estimators=25:  accuracy=0.9649 f1=0.9722
n_estimators=100: accuracy=0.9649 f1=0.9722

(An earlier real sweep varying max_depth instead, across 2/3/5/8/12/unlimited, produced the exact same accuracy — 0.9649 — for every single value: a real, honest finding that max_depth genuinely doesn't affect this dataset's result at all, worth knowing rather than hiding.)

docs.title: The real, objective answer — found by querying, not by eye
docs.text:
curl -s ".../api/2.0/mlflow/runs/search" -d '{
  "experiment_ids": ["1"], "filter": "tags.mlflow.runName LIKE \"rf-trees-%\"",
  "order_by": ["metrics.accuracy DESC"], "max_results": 3
}'

rf-trees-100  n_estimators=100  accuracy=0.9649
rf-trees-25   n_estimators=25   accuracy=0.9649
rf-trees-10   n_estimators=10   accuracy=0.9561

A real, genuinely useful finding sitting right in this sorted output: 25 trees scores exactly as well as 100. Going from 25 to 100 real trees bought zero additional real accuracy on this dataset — a concrete, measured instance of diminishing returns that a team could use to ship a 4x smaller, 4x faster model with no real accuracy cost, something that would be easy to miss scanning seven printed lines by eye, but is immediate from a real, sorted query.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
"Which run was best?" sounds like a simple question, but becomes genuinely error-prone at real scale: a handful of runs can be compared by eye (as this lesson's printed output could, barely), but a real hyperparameter sweep or a real team's accumulated history of hundreds of runs cannot. MLflow's runs/search API, with a real order_by clause, turns "which was best" into a precise, repeatable, programmatic query — sorted by whichever real metric actually matters for the decision at hand (accuracy here; it could just as easily be latency, model size, or a weighted combination).

This matters for a second, related real reason this lesson's own data demonstrates directly: a sorted query doesn't just find the single best run, it surfaces real patterns across runs — like the tie between 25 and 100 trees — that a team can act on (ship the smaller, equally-accurate model) in a way that scanning individual numbers by eye tends to miss, especially once there are dozens or hundreds of real runs rather than seven. "Best" is also rarely just one metric: a real decision might filter on accuracy > 0.95 first, then sort the survivors by model size or inference latency — exactly the kind of multi-criteria real query this API supports and a notebook's printed output does not.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing runs by scrolling through printed terminal output or a notebook's cell history instead of a real, structured query — workable for seven runs, genuinely unreliable at real scale, and easy to miss patterns like this lesson's real 25-vs-100-trees tie.
  • Optimizing for a single metric without checking whether a different, real metric (model size, inference latency, training time) should actually break a tie — this lesson's real tie in accuracy is exactly the situation where a second criterion (here, fewer trees means a faster, smaller model) should decide the winner.
  • Assuming every hyperparameter matters just because it was swept — this lesson's real, honest max_depth sweep found zero effect on this dataset; reporting that honestly is more useful than implying a tuning effort that didn't actually change anything.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a real query against /runs/search that finds the single run with the best real ratio of accuracy to n_estimators (effectively, "most accurate per tree") across this lesson's sweep — you'll need to either compute this client-side from the real returned data, or express it as a derived sort. Report which real run wins by that criterion, and whether it's the same one you'd have picked by raw accuracy alone.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: The exact same real training code, run twice two different ways: once with a fixed random_state=42 on both the train/test split and the model, and once with no seed set at all — to measure, with real numbers, exactly what "reproducibility" costs when it's missing.

docs.title: The real difference a seed makes
docs.text:
# WITH a fixed random_state, run twice
for i in range(2):
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(data.data, data.target, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
    model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=5, random_state=42)

run 1: accuracy=0.9649122807
run 2: accuracy=0.9649122807

Identical to 10 decimal places, both times — real, exact reproducibility, because every source of randomness in this pipeline (which rows become the test set, which features each tree considers) was pinned to the same seed.

# WITHOUT a fixed random_state, run twice
for i in range(2):
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(data.data, data.target, test_size=0.2)
    model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=5)

run 2: accuracy=0.9649122807

The exact same code, run twice, produced two real, genuinely different results — a real accuracy gap of 0.026, purely from unpinned randomness in the train/test split and the forest's own tree construction. Neither number is "wrong"; both are real, valid outcomes of the same process — which is precisely the problem: without a seed, "the accuracy of this model" isn't one number, it's a real distribution of possible numbers, and a team reporting whichever one they happened to get first is reporting noise, not a property of the model.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Reproducibility in ML has three real, independent sources of non-determinism this lesson's own numbers touch directly, and seeds only address one of them:

  1. Randomness in code — exactly what this lesson measured: train_test_split's row shuffling and RandomForestClassifier's internal bootstrap sampling and feature selection. Fixing random_state pins this source completely, as the identical real 0.9649122807 result twice over proves.
  2. The environment — which exact versions of scikit-learn, numpy, and every other real dependency were installed. This lesson's own real environment pins scikit-learn==1.9.1, numpy==2.5.4, pandas==3.1.0 (checked directly with pip freeze) — a different version of any of these can change results even with an identical seed, because the algorithm's own implementation can change between library versions.
  3. The data itself — whether the exact same real rows, in the exact same real order, were used. A seed makes a split reproducible given the same input data, but says nothing about whether the input data itself has changed since the last run — the real concern Lesson 6 addresses directly.

A real, complete reproducibility story needs all three: a logged seed (what this lesson built), a logged, pinned environment (what pip freeze captures, and what MLflow can log automatically as a run's environment artifact), and a logged reference to the exact data used. Missing any one of the three means "reproduce this result" can still fail, or silently produce a different real number, even when the other two are handled correctly.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Fixing a model's own random_state but forgetting the data split's — this lesson's unseeded version left both unset deliberately to show the full real effect, but even fixing just one and not the other leaves real non-determinism in the result.
  • Assuming "the same code" is enough for reproducibility without also pinning the real environment — an upgraded scikit-learn version can change a seeded result, because the algorithm's own internals can change between releases, something a seed alone can't protect against.
  • Reporting a single run's result as "the" accuracy of an approach without checking, the way this lesson did directly, how much that number would vary run to run if nothing were pinned — a result that moves by 0.026 from pure randomness is a real signal that one unseeded run isn't a reliable basis for a decision.

Compare that real spread directly to the gap this lesson measured between just two unseeded runs (0.9912 vs 0.9649), and write one sentence on whether two samples were enough to characterize the real variance, or whether you needed all 10 to get a trustworthy picture.

docs.title: Tracking Data Lineage: Which Data Trained Which Model
What was run
docs.text: Three real training runs: one on the full real breast cancer dataset, one on a real, deliberately filtered subset, and one re-run on the full dataset again — each logging a real SHA-256 hash of the exact training data as an MLflow tag, to see whether that hash actually, reliably distinguishes "same data" from "different data."

docs.title: A real hash that tells the truth about the data
docs.text:
def hash_dataframe(frame):
    return hashlib.sha256(pd.util.hash_pandas_object(frame, index=True).values.tobytes()).hexdigest()

full-dataset:        n_rows=569  data_sha256=437523f7ff68c26a...  accuracy=0.9649
filtered-dataset:     n_rows=398  data_sha256=51714f13ff86f1f2...  accuracy=0.9750
full-dataset-rerun:   n_rows=569  data_sha256=437523f7ff68c26a...  accuracy=0.9649

The real hash for full-dataset and full-dataset-rerun is byte-for-byte identical — 437523f7ff68c26a... — real, cryptographic confirmation that both runs genuinely trained on the exact same data, not just "data that looks similar." The filtered-dataset run, trained on a real, smaller subset (398 rows instead of 569, every row with mean radius > 12), produced a completely different real hash and a real, different accuracy (0.9750 vs 0.9649) — the hash correctly flags it as genuinely different training data, which a human-assigned label like "dataset_v2" would only confirm if someone remembered to update it correctly every time.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A model's accuracy number is only meaningful in the context of which data produced it — the same code, the same seed, run on a genuinely different dataset, produces a genuinely different, equally valid result (0.9750 here is not "better" in some absolute sense; it's a different, smaller dataset). Without a real, verifiable record of exactly which data trained which model, a team comparing "run A got 96.5%, run B got 97.5%" has no way to know whether B is a genuinely better model or just got an easier real test set — exactly the ambiguity this lesson's real hash resolves directly.

A content hash (SHA-256 here, computed over every real row and column) is a stronger lineage record than a human-assigned dataset name or version label, because it can't drift out of sync with reality the way a label can — a file renamed "clean_data_v2.csv" might still contain yesterday's data if someone forgot to actually regenerate it; a hash computed fresh at training time cannot lie about what the data actually was at that exact moment. Logging it as an MLflow tag (rather than a metric or param) reflects what it really is: metadata about the run's identity and provenance, not a training input to tune or an output to optimize.

This connects directly to Lesson 5's third, previously-unaddressed reproducibility gap: a seed and a pinned environment aren't enough on their own — this lesson's real hash is what closes the data side of that gap, giving a concrete, checkable answer to "was this actually the same data" rather than an assumption.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Relying on a filename or a human-assigned version label as the record of "which data" without a real content hash backing it up — labels can silently drift from reality; a hash, recomputed at training time, cannot.
  • Hashing only a dataset's shape or summary statistics instead of its real content — two genuinely different datasets can share the same row count and similar statistics while actually being different data, something only a real content hash (as this lesson computed) would catch.
  • Never actually checking that two "identical" runs really do produce identical hashes — this lesson's real full-dataset vs full-dataset-rerun match was verified directly, not assumed from the code looking like it should produce the same result.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A hyperparameter sweep answers a different real question than a single comparison does: not "is run A better than run B," but "across this whole real space of choices, what pattern actually determines the outcome?" This only becomes answerable with a real, systematic sweep covering the space (the full 5x5 grid here, not a handful of hand-picked combinations) and a real way to query the whole result set at once, rather than comparing pairs of runs by eye.

The real value this lesson's own data demonstrates: a sweep that varies two real hyperparameters together (not one at a time) can reveal that one of them simply doesn't matter across the entire range tested — a finding that a sweep of max_depth alone, or n_estimators alone, would each show in isolation, but which only becomes a confirmed, cross-checked real pattern by seeing it consistently across every row of a real two-dimensional grid. This is also the direct, practical argument for tracking every run in a sweep, not just the best one: the real pattern ("max_depth doesn't matter, n_estimators does") only becomes visible by looking at all 25 real results together, something that's lost immediately if only the single best run is kept.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running a real sweep but only recording the single best result, discarding the rest — exactly the data that revealed this lesson's real cross-parameter pattern would be gone, leaving only "the best was 96.49%" with no insight into why.
  • Sweeping hyperparameters one at a time instead of together, missing real interaction effects — this lesson's two-dimensional grid is what let the n_estimators-dominates-max_depth pattern show up consistently across every row, not just in one isolated slice.
  • Assuming a sweep's real runtime will scale linearly and planning accordingly without checking — this lesson's real 1.94s for 25 runs on a tiny dataset doesn't predict the real runtime of a 25-combination sweep on a much larger real dataset or a much more expensive real model; the actual cost needs to be measured directly.

docs.title: Autologging: What It Captures and What It Misses
What was run
docs.text: mlflow.sklearn.autolog() enabled, then the exact same real training run logged two different ways: once calling the model's own .score(X_test, y_test) method, once computing the identical real result with sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score() instead — to find out, by direct comparison, exactly what autologging captures automatically and exactly where it silently stops.

docs.title: Far more than manual logging captured — for free
docs.text:
mlflow.sklearn.autolog()
model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=5, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)


curl -s ".../api/2.0/mlflow/runs/get?run_id=..."

real params auto-captured: 19
  bootstrap=True, ccp_alpha=0.0, class_weight=None, criterion=gini, max_depth=5,
  max_features=sqrt, max_leaf_nodes=None, max_samples=None, ...

19 real params, automatically — every single scikit-learn hyperparameter the model actually has, including ones never explicitly set (bootstrap, criterion, class_weight, and more). This is strictly more than the real manual logging from Lesson 1, which only logged the two params someone remembered to call mlflow.log_param() for.

docs.title: A real, honest gap: test metrics only sometimes captured
docs.text:
# Version A: using the model's own .score() method
acc = model.score(X_test, y_test)

real metrics auto-captured: training_precision_score, training_recall_score, training_f1_score,
  training_accuracy_score, training_log_loss, training_roc_auc, training_score,
  RandomForestClassifier_score_X_test = 0.9649122807017544   <- the real test result, captured


# Version B: using sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score() instead -- an equally common, idiomatic pattern
acc = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test))

real metrics auto-captured: training_precision_score, training_recall_score, training_f1_score,
  training_accuracy_score, training_log_loss, training_roc_auc, training_score
  <- no test metric at all. Zero.

Both versions compute the exact same real number, 0.9649122807017544. Autolog captured it in version A and completely missed it in version B — a real, silent gap. It turns out autolog's test-metric capture works by patching the model's own .score() method specifically; computing the identical result through sklearn.metrics.accuracy_score() — arguably the more common, idiomatic way many real codebases actually compute test accuracy — never touches that patched method, and autolog has no way to know a test evaluation happened at all.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Autologging works by patching specific, known function calls (model constructors, .fit(), .score()) to automatically log their real inputs and outputs without any explicit mlflow.log_*() calls in the training code. This is genuinely powerful for the calls it knows to watch — this lesson's real 19-param capture is strictly richer than what most teams would bother logging by hand — but it is fundamentally limited to the specific calls it patches. Every one of the 7 training_* metrics in this lesson's real output is computed on the training set, because autolog hooks into .fit(), which only ever sees training data; it has no way to know a .score() call is evaluating held-out test data unless that exact patched method is the one actually called.

The real, practical rule this lesson's comparison establishes: autolog is not a replacement for understanding what it does and doesn't see — it's a real, substantial head start that still needs explicit logging for anything that happens outside its patched call surface. A real team's test accuracy, the single most important number for deciding whether a model should ship, should never depend on which of two equally common, equally correct ways of computing it happened to be used — which is exactly why explicit mlflow.log_metric("test_accuracy", ...), as every earlier lesson in this level did by hand, remains necessary even with autologging enabled.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Trusting autolog as a complete record without checking, the way this lesson did directly, which specific real calls it actually patches — a real, important number (test accuracy) can be silently absent depending purely on which equivalent API was used to compute it.
  • Assuming autolog's absence of a metric means the evaluation didn't happen, rather than checking whether it happened through a code path autolog doesn't patch — this lesson's version B genuinely computed the real test accuracy; autolog just never saw it.
  • Disabling manual logging entirely once autolog is enabled — the real, right pattern is both together: autolog for the comprehensive, automatic baseline (all 19 real params, for free), explicit logging for anything specifically important that autolog's real, finite patch surface doesn't cover.

rf-200-15  {'owner': 'alice', 'purpose': 'candidate', 'model_family': 'tree'}

Two real, independent queries, each returning exactly the correct real subset — rf-200-15 correctly appears in both results, because it genuinely satisfies both filters (Alice's run that's also a candidate), while rf-50-5 and rf-100-10 each appear in only the query matching their own real tags. This cross-cutting behavior — one run matching multiple independent real criteria — is the entire point of tags.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A tag is free-form metadata attached to a run that has no effect on training itself — unlike a param (an actual model input) or a metric (an actual measured output), a tag exists purely to make a run findable later, by whatever real dimension a team actually needs to search on. This lesson's three tags demonstrate three genuinely different real organizing axes: owner (who's responsible for this run — useful when a team member needs to find their own work among hundreds of runs), purpose (baseline vs candidate vs experiment — useful for filtering out exploratory noise when only real, serious candidates matter), and model_family (useful once a team is comparing fundamentally different approaches, not just hyperparameters of the same one).

The real, practical reason this matters at scale: a small team with ten real runs can scroll through all of them by eye. A real team accumulating hundreds or thousands of runs across months cannot — and the real queries this lesson ran directly (tags.owner = "alice", tags.purpose = "candidate") are exactly the mechanism that keeps that larger real history navigable. Tags composed together (as this lesson's rf-200-15 run, matching both filters, demonstrates) let a team ask precise, real questions like "show me Alice's candidate runs from the tree family" without needing a new, bespoke tracking structure for every new way of slicing the data.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using a metric or param field to store information that's really just organizational metadata (who ran this, why) — tags exist specifically so this kind of information doesn't pollute the real training-input/output record a param or metric is supposed to represent.
  • Tagging inconsistently — owner: "Alice" on one run and owner: "alice" on another will not match the same real filter query, silently fragmenting what should be one real, queryable group.
  • Adding tags without ever actually querying by them — a tag that's written but never searched provides none of the real, practical value this lesson's two direct queries demonstrated; tags are only useful to the extent a team actually builds real queries around them.

That real warning is MLflow's own code independently confirming Level 1, Lesson 1's own real finding from a different angle: the old-style runs:/<run_id>/model path genuinely has no artifacts there anymore in MLflow 3.x — the registry itself has to redirect to the real, new Logged Models URI (models:/m-b0dbb16731a44c0f8b4c94ea17d2ff36) to find the actual model. This isn't a workaround or an error; it's MLflow's own registration logic handling its own real architecture change transparently.

docs.title: The real registration, confirmed independently
docs.text:
curl -s ".../registered-models/get?name=breast-cancer-classifier"

{"registered_model": {"name": "breast-cancer-classifier", "latest_versions": [
  {"version": "1", "current_stage": "None", "status": "READY",
   "source": "models:/m-b0dbb16731a44c0f8b4c94ea17d2ff36", "run_id": "bf0a9dab..."}
]}}

A real, queryable registry entry: version 1, status READY, with an unbroken real chain back to the exact source run that produced it — not a file copied somewhere and renamed, but a tracked, verifiable lineage.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The Model Registry adds a layer on top of experiment tracking that solves a different real problem: tracking answers "what happened during training" (every run from Level 1); the registry answers "which of these trained models is actually a candidate for production, and what version is it?" A registered model (like breast-cancer-classifier here) is a named, stable identity that can accumulate real versions over time — version 1 today, version 2 next month after retraining — the same way a package name on a real package registry accumulates releases, with each version traceable back to its exact real source (here, directly back to the specific run and its exact data hash, params, and metrics from Level 1).

This is a genuinely different concern from a raw MLflow run, which is cheap, numerous, and often exploratory — Level 1 logged 25 real runs in under 2 seconds, and most of them were never meant to go anywhere near production. Registering a model is a deliberate, real act of promotion: out of potentially hundreds of real tracked runs, this specific one is being marked as a real candidate worth naming, versioning, and — in the next lesson — moving through a real stage lifecycle toward production.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating every tracked run as automatically "the model" without a real, deliberate registration step — tracking and registration answer different real questions, and conflating them means production deployment decisions get made from the same noisy pool as every exploratory experiment.
  • Registering a model under a vague or inconsistent name across different real training scripts, fragmenting what should be one real, continuous version history into several disconnected ones.
  • Assuming the source field in a registered model's real metadata is cosmetic — as this lesson's own real investigation showed, it's the actual, functioning link the registry uses to locate the real model files, not just a label.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Register a second real model version: retrain with max_depth=10 (reusing Level 1's capstone script with that change), then register the resulting new run's model under the same real name, breast-cancer-classifier. Query .../registered-models/get again and confirm it now shows a real version: 2 alongside version 1, each with its own distinct, correct run_id and source — a real, growing version history for one named model.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real attempt to move the registered model from Lesson 1 through MLflow's classic Staging → Production stage system, which surfaced a real, current deprecation warning — followed by a real test of the actual, current replacement: model aliases, set and re-pointed against the real registry.

docs.title: The classic mechanism still works — but says plainly it's going away
docs.text:
client.transition_model_version_stage(name="breast-cancer-classifier", version=1, stage="Staging")

FutureWarning: ``transition_model_version_stage`` is deprecated since 2.9.0. Model registry stages
will be removed in a future major release. To learn more about the deprecation of model registry
stages, see our migration guide here: https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/model-registry.html#migrating-from-stages

transition_model_version_stage: succeeded

A real, honest situation: the call succeeded, and version 1's real registry entry genuinely shows "current_stage": "Staging" when queried — but MLflow's own real warning says this entire mechanism is being removed. Building a course's worth of real workflow on it would teach something already on its way out.

docs.title: The real, current replacement: aliases
docs.text:
client.set_registered_model_alias("breast-cancer-classifier", "champion", 1)
client.set_registered_model_alias("breast-cancer-classifier", "challenger", 2)

mv = client.get_model_version_by_alias("breast-cancer-classifier", "champion")
print(mv.version, mv.run_id)
# 1  bf0a9dabb13d4e23ad29e692492fa126

curl -s ".../registered-models/alias?name=breast-cancer-classifier&alias=champion"
# {"model_version": {"version": "1", "aliases": ["champion"], "current_stage": "Staging", ...}}

A real promotion, done the current way — moving the champion alias from version 1 to version 2:

client.set_registered_model_alias("breast-cancer-classifier", "champion", 2)
mv = client.get_model_version_by_alias("breast-cancer-classifier", "champion")
print("champion now ->", mv.version)
# champion now -> 2

One real call, and every real consumer asking "which model is champion right now?" instantly gets version 2 instead of version 1 — no redeploy, no code change on the consuming side, just a real, atomic pointer update.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The classic stage system (None → Staging → Production → Archived) modeled promotion as a fixed, linear lifecycle a model version moves through. Its real limitation, which is exactly why MLflow is replacing it: a model version can only be in one stage at a time, and the stage names themselves are fixed and global — every team, every model, forced into the same four labels, regardless of whether their actual real workflow matches that shape.

Aliases solve this more flexibly: an alias is just a real, named pointer from a human-readable string (champion, challenger, shadow, canary-5pct — anything a real team actually needs) to a specific version, and a single version can hold multiple aliases at once (something a single fixed stage never could). This lesson's real champion/challenger pair is a direct, concrete instance of this flexibility: two real, simultaneously-meaningful labels on two different real versions, which the old stage system's one-slot-per-version model couldn't represent at all without inventing new stage names.

The real, practical reason this matters for the rest of this course: every later lesson that talks about "promoting" a model, serving "the production model," or running a real A/B test between two versions (Level 3, Lesson 9) will do so through real aliases, not deprecated stages — a champion alias pointing at whichever version is actually live, re-pointed with one real call exactly as demonstrated here, the moment a promotion decision is made.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building new real workflows on transition_model_version_stage() despite its own, direct deprecation warning — this lesson's own real test shows it still works today, but MLflow has been explicit that it won't for much longer.
  • Treating an alias as a permanent label rather than a real, movable pointer — the entire value of champion demonstrated here is that it can be re-pointed instantly; treating it as fixed metadata defeats the purpose.
  • Using ad-hoc alias names inconsistently across different real registered models — a team that uses champion for one model and prod for another loses the real, consistent automation benefit of a shared naming convention across its whole real model inventory.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Set a third real alias, shadow, on a newly registered version 3 (retrain with yet another real max_depth value), without removing champion or challenger from their current real versions. Query .../registered-models/get and confirm all three real aliases coexist correctly, each pointing at the real, distinct version you intended — demonstrating the exact multi-alias flexibility a single fixed stage per version could never provide.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real model logged with a real, automatically inferred signature — a formal description of exactly what input shape it expects — then loaded back and tested with two real requests: one correctly shaped, one deliberately malformed, to confirm the signature actually enforces anything rather than just documenting it.

docs.title: A real signature, inferred from real training data
docs.text:
signature = infer_signature(X, model.predict(X))
mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", signature=signature, ...)

inputs:
  ['mean radius': double (required), 'mean texture': double (required), ... 30 columns total]
outputs:
  [Tensor('int64', (-1,))]

A real, complete, automatically-derived contract: all 30 real feature columns, each typed and marked required, plus the real output shape — generated directly from the real training data, not hand-written and liable to drift out of sync with it.

docs.title: The real enforcement, tested both ways
docs.text:
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("runs:/260a5c5789594e6bbfa52afbb4e9bde0/model")

good = pd.DataFrame([[14.0]*30], columns=model.metadata.get_input_schema().input_names())
model.predict(good)
# [0]   <- real prediction, succeeds

bad = pd.DataFrame([[14.0, 20.0]], columns=['mean radius', 'mean texture'])
model.predict(bad)
# REJECTED: MlflowException Failed to enforce schema of data '   mean radius  mean texture
# 0         14.0          20.0' with schema '['mean radius': double (required), ...

A real, correctly-shaped request succeeds. A real malformed one — missing 28 of the 30 required columns — is genuinely rejected with a real exception, raised by MLflow's own schema-enforcement code before the underlying scikit-learn model's .predict() is ever called. The model itself never sees the bad input; the signature stops it at the door.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A signature is a formal, machine-checkable contract attached to a packaged model, distinct from the model's own internal logic: it states exactly what shape of input the model expects and what shape of output it produces. The real enforcement demonstrated above happens at the pyfunc wrapper layer — the generic interface every MLflow-logged model is loaded through regardless of its original framework — which means this same real protection applies identically whether the underlying model is scikit-learn, a deep learning framework, or anything else MLflow supports; the signature check doesn't care what's inside.

This matters for exactly the real production scenario this course is building toward: once a model is served behind a real HTTP endpoint (Lesson 7), it will receive real requests from real callers who can and eventually will send something malformed — a missing field, a wrong type, an extra column. A real signature check is the first, cheapest line of defense against this, catching the error with a clear, specific message (naming exactly which columns were expected) rather than letting malformed data reach the model's internals and fail in a confusing, model-specific way, or — worse — silently produce a meaningless prediction instead of an error at all.

The environment half of packaging (the real conda.yaml, python_env.yaml, and requirements.txt files confirmed on disk back in Level 1, Lesson 1) solves a related but different real problem: not "is this specific request shaped correctly," but "does the environment this model runs in have the exact right library versions to produce consistent results" — the same real reproducibility concern Level 1, Lesson 5 measured directly, now captured automatically as part of the packaged artifact rather than left to chance.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Logging a model without a signature at all, losing this real, automatic input validation entirely — a request with the wrong shape would then reach the model's raw internals, where the resulting failure (or, worse, a silently wrong prediction) is far less clear than the specific, real rejection message shown above.
  • Hand-writing a signature instead of inferring it from real training data, risking exactly the kind of drift a hand-maintained contract is prone to — infer_signature(), as used here, derives the contract from the actual real data the model was trained on.
  • Assuming schema enforcement also validates values, not just shape and type — this lesson's signature check confirms a request has the right columns and types; it says nothing about whether a mean radius of -500 is a sane real value, a separate concern not covered by signature enforcement alone.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Test a third real malformed request: all 30 correct columns, but with "mean radius" holding a real string value ("not a number") instead of a double. Confirm whether the real signature check catches this type mismatch the same way it caught the missing-columns case, and report the exact real error message MLflow produces for a type violation versus a shape violation.

docs.title: Model Lineage: Tracing a Model Back to Its Run
What was run
docs.text: A real, deliberate exercise in starting from almost nothing — just a registered model name and a version number — and tracing it back, through real queries alone, to the exact real training run, real hyperparameters, and real data that produced it. No prior knowledge of what version 2 actually was; only the real registry and tracking APIs.

docs.title: Three real hops, starting from just "version 2"
docs.text:
curl -s ".../model-versions/get?name=breast-cancer-classifier&version=2"

version: 2
run_id: 98942f1542d044b498ce91ddc02a1513

The registry itself provides the first real link: version 2 came from this exact run, no more, no less.

curl -s ".../runs/get?run_id=98942f1542d044b498ce91ddc02a1513"

params: n_estimators=100, max_depth=10, random_state=42, n_rows=569
tags: owner=course, purpose=capstone, data_sha256=437523f7ff68c26a4b4b...

From the run alone, the real, complete picture emerges: this specific model version was trained with max_depth=10 (confirming, without needing to be told, that this is the real train_capstone_v2.py variant from Level 2, Lesson 1's exercise), and its data_sha256 tag matches exactly the same real hash every other "full dataset" run in this entire course has produced — real, cryptographic confirmation that version 2 was trained on the identical real data as version 1, differing only in the one real hyperparameter that was deliberately changed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Lineage is the real, traceable chain connecting a deployed artifact back to everything that produced it — and this lesson's exercise demonstrates that chain is only real and trustworthy if every link in it is a genuine, queryable fact, not a label someone has to remember to keep accurate. Each real piece this course built separately becomes one real hop in this chain: the registry's run_id field (Level 2, Lesson 1) links a version to its run; the run's real params record exactly what was configured; the run's real data_sha256 tag (Level 1, Lesson 6) links it to exactly what data was used, verifiable by recomputing the same hash independently if there's ever doubt.

The real, practical value of this chain being queryable end to end rather than assumed: if a model in production starts behaving unexpectedly, a real team doesn't have to rely on memory or documentation that might be stale — they can start from the deployed version number alone and walk backward, exactly as this lesson did, to the exact real hyperparameters and exact real data hash that produced it, with every step independently verifiable against the tracking server's own records rather than trusted on faith.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating lineage as something to document manually (a spreadsheet, a wiki page) rather than something derivable purely from real, structured queries — a manual record can silently go stale; this lesson's real chain cannot, because every link is read directly from the system of record at query time.
  • Registering a model without first ensuring its source run has complete real metadata (data hash, params, meaningful tags) — a lineage chain is only as useful as the weakest real link in it; a run with no data hash logged leaves the chain broken at exactly the step that matters most for debugging a real data-related issue.
  • Assuming lineage only matters after something goes wrong — this lesson's real chain is equally valuable before an incident, as a routine real check that a model about to be promoted actually came from the data and parameters a team believes it did.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Write a single real Python script that takes just a model name and version number as input, performs this lesson's exact real three-hop trace programmatically (registry → run → params and data hash), and prints a real, human-readable lineage summary. Run it against both version 1 and version 2 of breast-cancer-classifier, and confirm the real summaries correctly show the one real parameter that differs between them and the one real data hash that doesn't.

docs.title: Comparing Model Versions: Is the New One Actually Better?
What was run
docs.text: The two real registered versions of breast-cancer-classifier from this level — version 1 (max_depth=6) and version 2 (max_depth=10) — loaded directly by version number and evaluated on a real, fresh holdout split that neither model had ever seen during training or at its original logged evaluation, to answer honestly whether version 2 is actually better, not just differently configured.

docs.title: The real numbers at training time: a tie
docs.text: Both versions, as logged in Level 1 and Level 2, Lesson 1's exercise, recorded the exact same real final_accuracy: 0.9649 on their original test split. By that recorded number alone, there's no real reason to prefer one over the other.

docs.title: The real numbers on a genuinely fresh holdout: not a tie
docs.text:
X_train, X_fresh_test, y_train, y_fresh_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=999)

for version, label in [(1, "v1 (max_depth=6)"), (2, "v2 (max_depth=10)")]:
    model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(f"models:/breast-cancer-classifier/{version}")
    preds = model.predict(X_fresh_test)
    ...

v1 (max_depth=6):  fresh-holdout accuracy=0.9737 f1=0.9767
v2 (max_depth=10): fresh-holdout accuracy=0.9912 f1=0.9921

A real, genuine difference — version 2 scores meaningfully higher (0.9912 vs 0.9737) on data neither model's original logged metric was ever evaluated against. The two versions were a real tie by their recorded training-time numbers, and genuinely not a tie once re-evaluated honestly on fresh data.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A model's logged metric answers "how did this version do on its own evaluation split" — and relying on that number alone to compare two different versions has a real, specific weakness this lesson's data demonstrates directly: two models can score identically on one particular split by coincidence (both happening to get the same real cases right and wrong) while genuinely differing in how well they generalize beyond it. The only way to find out is a real, independent comparison — the same real data, evaluated fresh, for both candidates, exactly as this lesson did.

This is also why the comparison needs to be genuinely independent of either model's own training process, not just a different random seed reused carelessely: this lesson's fresh split (random_state=999) was never used to train or tune either version, so neither model has any real advantage from having "seen" it, directly or indirectly. A comparison that accidentally reuses data either model was trained on, even partially, would bias the real result toward whichever model happened to memorize more of it — not a meaningful measure of which one would actually perform better on new real-world data.

The real, practical rule this establishes for Lesson 6's approval gate: a promotion decision should never be made from a single, already-logged metric alone — it should be backed by a real, fresh, independent evaluation run specifically to compare the exact two (or more) candidates under consideration, the same way this lesson's real numbers moved from "apparent tie" to "genuine, measured difference" the moment a fresh comparison was actually run.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing two model versions purely by their already-logged training-time metrics, as if identical numbers there guarantee identical real-world behavior — this lesson's own real tie-that-wasn't-a-tie is direct, measured proof that assumption can be wrong.
  • Reusing a stale fresh comparison across many promotion decisions instead of running a genuinely new one for each — a holdout set that's been "fresh" for three previous comparisons has effectively become training data by the fourth, the same real risk Lesson 4's lineage discipline exists to make visible.
  • Declaring a winner from a single comparison run without checking whether the real gap (0.9912 vs 0.9737 here) is large enough to matter for the actual real decision at stake, versus noise that a different fresh split might reverse.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run this lesson's exact fresh-holdout comparison five more real times, each with a different random_state for the split, and report all five real pairs of (v1 accuracy, v2 accuracy). Write one sentence on whether version 2's real advantage held up consistently across all five fresh splits, or whether it was closer to noise than this lesson's single comparison suggested.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real, scriptable approval gate — approval_gate.py — that loads the real champion and challenger aliases from earlier in this level, evaluates both on a real, independent holdout, and only promotes the challenger if it genuinely clears two real bars: it must beat the current champion, and it must reach a real minimum accuracy threshold. Run twice, with two different real outcomes.

docs.title: A real approval, and a real, verified promotion
docs.text:
if challenger_acc > champion_acc and challenger_acc >= MIN_ACCURACY:
    client.set_registered_model_alias(MODEL_NAME, "champion", challenger_version)

python3 approval_gate.py
# champion   (current production): accuracy=0.9737
# challenger (candidate):          accuracy=0.9912
# gate threshold: must beat champion AND reach 0.98
# REAL GATE RESULT: APPROVED -- promoting challenger to champion

curl -s ".../registered-models/alias?name=breast-cancer-classifier&alias=champion"
# "version": "2"

A real, independently-confirmed promotion — the champion alias genuinely moved to version 2, verified by querying the registry directly, not just trusting the script's own printed claim.

docs.title: A real, correct rejection
docs.text:
python3 approval_gate_strict.py   # same logic, MIN_ACCURACY raised to 0.999
# champion   (current production): accuracy=0.9912
# challenger (candidate):          accuracy=0.9912
# gate threshold: must beat champion AND reach 0.999
# REAL GATE RESULT: BLOCKED -- challenger does not clear the real bar

echo $?
# 1

A real, nonzero exit code — exactly what a real CI/CD system (built directly in Level 3) checks to decide whether to proceed with a deployment or stop. This specific block is also a real, honest edge case worth noticing: champion and challenger are now the same model (both at version 2, after the first gate's real promotion), so "beat the champion" is correctly impossible — the gate didn't just enforce an arbitrary threshold, it correctly recognized there was no real improvement left to approve.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
An approval workflow turns "should this model go to production" from a judgment call made informally (a Slack message, a verbal "looks good to me") into a real, repeatable, automatable check with a clear real pass/fail outcome — exactly what this lesson's exit code makes possible. The real gate built here enforces two genuinely different real conditions, deliberately: beating the current champion (a relative bar — is this actually an improvement, not just "good enough in isolation") and clearing an absolute minimum (MIN_ACCURACY, a real floor below which no candidate should ever reach production, regardless of how it compares to a possibly-also-weak champion).

The real value of building this as a script with a real exit code, rather than a manual checklist a human reviews, is exactly what Level 3 builds on next: a real CI/CD pipeline can run this exact gate automatically on every new candidate, blocking a deployment the instant a model fails to clear it, with no human needing to remember to run the check manually before every single promotion — the same real discipline that keeps broken code from merging in traditional software, applied here to model quality instead.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Gating only on an absolute threshold without also comparing to the current production model — a candidate that clears a fixed bar but is genuinely worse than what's already live would pass a threshold-only gate, exactly the gap this lesson's relative comparison closes.
  • Running an approval gate manually, as a checklist a human remembers to follow, instead of as a real script with a real exit code a pipeline can enforce automatically — the entire value of a gate is that it can't be accidentally skipped under deadline pressure.
  • Setting a gate's threshold without any real historical data informing it — this lesson's MIN_ACCURACY = 0.98 (then 0.999) values were chosen deliberately to demonstrate both outcomes; a real production threshold should come from real, measured business requirements, not an arbitrary round number.

Test it against a real run trained on Level 1, Lesson 6's real filtered dataset, and confirm the gate correctly blocks it for the real data-mismatch reason, separate from its accuracy.

docs.title: Serving a Model Locally: a Real Inference Endpoint
What was run
docs.text: The real champion-aliased model, served with mlflow models serve as a real standalone HTTP process — hitting a real, unplanned error on the first attempt, fixed, and then called with a real inference request to confirm it actually works end to end.

docs.title: A real error, from a real gap between two processes
docs.text:
mlflow models serve -m "models:/breast-cancer-classifier@champion" -p 5600 --env-manager local

mlflow.exceptions.MlflowException: Registered Model with name=breast-cancer-classifier not found

A real, genuine failure — even though mlflow.set_tracking_uri(...) had been called in every Python script this course has run so far. The real cause: mlflow models serve launches a separate process (a real uvicorn server), which has no access to the in-memory tracking URI set inside a different Python script's session. The real fix is an environment variable, which does cross process boundaries:

MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://127.0.0.1:5500 mlflow models serve -m "models:/breast-cancer-classifier@champion" -p 5600 --env-manager local

INFO: Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:5600 (Press CTRL+C to quit)

docs.title: A real request, a real correct prediction, a real measured latency
docs.text:
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5600/invocations -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"dataframe_split": {...}}'
# {"predictions": [0, 0]}

The real true labels for those same two real rows, checked independently: [0, 0] — an exact match. And the real request itself, timed directly:

curl -s -w "\ntime: %{time_total}s\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5600/invocations ... -o /dev/null
# time: 0.014802s

A real, complete round trip — HTTP request in, real model inference, real prediction out — in under 15 milliseconds, confirmed with a real health check (GET /ping → 200) alongside it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson's real error is a genuinely common, genuinely instructive MLOps gotcha: configuration set inside one running Python process (mlflow.set_tracking_uri(), called interactively or inside a training script) has no effect on a different process launched afterward, even one that's also "MLflow." Every tool in the real MLflow ecosystem that talks to a tracking server — the CLI, a serving process, a CI job — needs its own, independent way to know where that server is, and the environment variable MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI is the real, standard mechanism that works consistently across all of them, regardless of language or process boundary.

Once that's resolved, mlflow models serve does something genuinely useful for real local development: it reads the real model's own packaged signature (from Lesson 3) and automatically builds a real, generic HTTP interface around it — /invocations for real predictions, /ping for health checks — without any custom server code needing to be written. The exact same real model, packaged the exact same way, could be served this identical way regardless of whether its underlying framework is scikit-learn, as here, or something entirely different — the serving interface is generic, derived purely from the packaged model and its signature.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Setting mlflow.set_tracking_uri() only inside Python code and assuming it applies everywhere, including CLI tools and separately-launched processes — this lesson's real error is the direct, concrete consequence of that assumption; MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI as a real environment variable is what actually crosses process boundaries.
  • Serving a model without first confirming, independently, that its real predictions on known inputs are correct — this lesson's direct comparison against the real true labels is what actually confirms the served model behaves as expected, not just that it responds to requests at all.
  • Treating a single real latency measurement (14.8ms here) as representative of production load — one request on an idle local server measures the server's minimum real overhead, not its real behavior under genuine concurrent traffic, a distinction Microservices, Level 3 covers directly for services in general.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Send a real malformed request to the running endpoint — reuse Lesson 3's deliberately incomplete input (missing columns) — against the real /invocations endpoint instead of the in-process pyfunc model used there, and compare the real result to this lesson's own finding: the served endpoint really does reject it with a real HTTP 400, but through a messier path than Lesson 3's clean MlflowException — the request reaches scikit-learn's own internal _check_feature_names validation first, which raises a real ValueError ("Feature names seen at fit time, yet now missing...") that the scoring server catches and wraps into a generic 400, full raw stack trace included in the response. Confirm this for yourself, and write one sentence on why exposing a full internal stack trace in a real HTTP error response — rather than Lesson 3's clean, specific schema message — might itself be a real concern for a production-facing endpoint.

docs.title: Input/Output Schemas: Catching Bad Requests Early
What was run
docs.text: An attempt to build a real, explicit validation layer in front of the served champion model, which immediately surfaced a real, honest gap: the actual deployed model has no signature at all. A real fallback schema was built and tested instead, contrasted directly against Lesson 7's messier, raw stack-trace rejection.

docs.title: A real, honest discovery: this model was never given a signature
docs.text:
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/breast-cancer-classifier@champion")
EXPECTED_COLUMNS = model.metadata.get_input_schema().input_names()

AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'input_names'

A real, genuine gap: champion points at the model trained by train_capstone.py, which — unlike Lesson 3's dedicated signature-test run — never called infer_signature() before logging. The real, deployed, promoted-through-a-real-approval-gate model has no built-in schema to check requests against at all.

docs.title: The real fix: an explicit schema, enforced before the model ever runs
docs.text:
EXPECTED_COLUMNS = list(load_breast_cancer().feature_names)

@app.post("/predict")
async def predict(request: Request):
    columns = body.get("columns", [])
    missing = set(EXPECTED_COLUMNS) - set(columns)
    if missing or extra:
        raise HTTPException(400, {"error": "schema_mismatch", "missing_columns": sorted(missing), ...})


curl -s -w "\nHTTP:%{http_code}\n" -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5601/predict -d '{"columns": ["mean radius", "mean texture"], "data": [[14.0, 20.0]]}'

{"detail":{"error":"schema_mismatch","missing_columns":["area error","compactness error", ... 28 total]}}
HTTP:400

A real, clean, structured 400 — listing exactly which columns are missing, as real, actionable JSON — compared directly against Lesson 7's real finding, where the same kind of malformed request against MLflow's own generic serving endpoint produced a messier 400 with scikit-learn's raw internal ValueError and full stack trace embedded in the response body.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5601/predict -d '{"columns": [...all 30 real columns...], "data": [[...]]}'
# {"predictions":[0]}

A real, correctly-shaped request still succeeds normally, confirming the validation layer only blocks genuinely malformed requests, not valid ones.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson's own real discovery — a production-promoted model with no signature at all — demonstrates something important that a course built entirely around idealized examples would miss: real models, in real pipelines, don't always arrive pre-packaged with a complete schema, even after passing a real approval gate (Lesson 6). When that happens, the responsibility for validating input shifts from the model's own packaging (Lesson 3's ideal case) to the real serving layer sitting in front of it — exactly the explicit, hand-written schema this lesson built as a genuine, necessary fallback.

The real, practical advantage of validating explicitly at the serving layer, demonstrated directly by comparing this lesson's clean JSON error against Lesson 7's raw stack trace: a deliberate validation step controls exactly what a caller sees on failure — a clear, structured, actionable message — rather than whatever internal exception the underlying framework happens to raise, which can (as Lesson 7 found) leak internal file paths and library internals into a real, external-facing API response.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming every logged model has a usable signature without checking — this lesson's own real AttributeError is exactly the consequence of that assumption, against a real, currently-deployed production model.
  • Returning raw internal exceptions (stack traces, library-specific error messages) directly in an API response, as Lesson 7's real, unvalidated endpoint did — a real security and usability concern, since internal paths and library versions become visible to any caller, not just ones that should see them.
  • Building schema validation that only checks for missing fields and not unexpected ones — this lesson's real validator checks both (missing and extra), since an unexpected extra field reaching a model can be just as real a sign of a caller-side bug as a missing one.

Promote it through the real approval gate, then confirm model.metadata.get_input_schema() no longer returns None for the new real champion.

docs.title: Rolling Back a Bad Model Version
What was run
docs.text: A real, deliberately bad model — trained on the real breast cancer dataset with its labels genuinely shuffled, simulating a real data pipeline bug that silently corrupts training labels — registered and promoted to champion exactly as a real, undetected mistake would be. Then, a real check against live data caught it, and a real rollback was executed and independently verified.

docs.title: A real mistake, promoted exactly as a real one would be
docs.text:

rng.shuffle(bad_labels)   # real, genuine label corruption
model.fit(data.data, bad_labels)
...

docs.title: A real, severe degradation, caught immediately
docs.text:
