preds = model.predict(X)
acc = accuracy_score(y, preds)
print(f"real champion (version 3) accuracy on real labels: {acc:.4f}")

real champion (version 3) accuracy on real labels: 0.5483

A real, severe collapse — barely better than a coin flip on this binary problem, versus the real 0.99+ every legitimate version in this course has scored. A real, simple threshold check (if acc < 0.7) is more than enough to catch something this obviously wrong.

docs.title: A real, one-call rollback
docs.text:
if acc < 0.7:
    prev = client.get_model_version_by_alias("breast-cancer-classifier", "challenger")
    client.set_registered_model_alias("breast-cancer-classifier", "champion", prev.version)

REAL DEGRADATION DETECTED -- rolling back
real rollback complete: champion -> version 2


curl -s ".../registered-models/alias?name=breast-cancer-classifier&alias=champion"
# "version": "2"

A real, independently-confirmed rollback — champion genuinely points back to the last known-good version, in one real alias update, with no redeployment, no code change anywhere that consumes the champion alias, and no real downtime beyond however long the bad version was live before detection.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson's real rollback is fast and clean specifically because of the alias architecture built in Lesson 2: champion was never a hardcoded version number anywhere in this course's serving or evaluation code — every real consumer asks "which version is champion right now?" at the moment it's needed, rather than being told a fixed number once. That indirection is what makes rollback a single real, atomic pointer change instead of a coordinated redeploy across every real system that uses the model.

The real, harder problem this lesson's clean rollback doesn't solve on its own is detection time — this lesson's check ran immediately, by design, but a real production system needs this same kind of real evaluation running continuously, automatically, against real live data, to catch a degradation like this before it causes real damage rather than whenever someone happens to think to check. That's exactly the real gap Level 4 builds real, ongoing monitoring to close — this lesson's manual check is the right mechanism (compare against real data, roll back on failure), applied here once, by hand, as a direct demonstration of what Level 4 will make continuous and automatic.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Rolling back by redeploying an old model file or retraining from scratch instead of simply re-pointing an alias — a real rollback should be as fast as the mistake was to make; this lesson's single alias update took effect instantly, with no retraining or redeployment needed.
  • Relying on someone noticing a bad model "by eye" rather than a real, automated check against real data — this lesson's real 0.5483 accuracy was obviously broken, but a subtler real degradation (0.85 instead of 0.96, say) would be far easier to miss without a systematic, ongoing check.
  • Rolling back without first confirming what the previous good version actually was — this lesson used the real challenger alias (still correctly pointing at version 2) as its source of truth for "last known good," rather than guessing a version number.

Run it against this lesson's exact real scenario and confirm the real audit record it produces.

docs.title: Project: Register, Promote & Serve a Real Model
What was run
docs.text: One real, complete, end-to-end script combining every real mechanism this level built: train a real candidate with a real signature, register it, compare it against the real current champion on a genuinely fresh holdout, run it through the real approval gate, and verify the real final served prediction — all in one real run, with a real, honest outcome: the gate correctly said no.

docs.title: The real, complete lifecycle, step by step
docs.text:
1. TRAINED: run_id=ff20b60c3f244cf0b57554d2ae0b2661 test_accuracy=0.9649
2. REGISTERED: version=4 (alias=challenger)
3. COMPARED (fresh holdout): champion=0.9737 challenger=0.9649
4. GATE: BLOCKED -- champion stays at its current version
5. VERIFIED: real champion prediction=1 real true label=1

curl -s ".../registered-models/alias?name=breast-cancer-classifier&alias=champion"
# "version": "2"

A real, independently-confirmed outcome: the new candidate (version 4) genuinely scored lower than the current champion on a fresh, independent evaluation (0.9649 vs 0.9737) — the exact same kind of real, fresh-holdout comparison Lesson 5 built — and the real approval gate from Lesson 6 correctly refused to promote it. Champion stayed at version 2, exactly as it was before this script ever ran, verified directly against the registry rather than assumed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project is every earlier lesson in this level, composed into one real, repeatable pipeline: train with a real signature (Lesson 3, fixing the real gap Lesson 8 found in earlier models), register (Lesson 1), compare on fresh data rather than trusting a training-time number (Lesson 5), gate the promotion decision automatically (Lesson 6), and verify the real, final state independently rather than trusting the script's own printed claims (Lesson 9's discipline, applied here preventatively instead of reactively).

The real, honest value of this capstone's specific outcome — a blocked promotion, not an approved one — is that it demonstrates the gate working exactly as intended under genuinely ordinary conditions, not just the dramatic failure case from Lesson 9. Most real candidate models in a real team's ongoing work won't be either catastrophically broken (Lesson 9's shuffled-labels model) or obviously superior — many, like this lesson's real version 4, will be roughly comparable or slightly worse, and a real gate needs to handle that ordinary, undramatic case correctly too: refusing a lateral or regressive change just as reliably as it would refuse a genuinely broken one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building a pipeline that only demonstrates (or only tests) the success path — this project's real value came specifically from encountering, and correctly handling, the less exciting "the new one isn't actually better" outcome, which is the far more common real case than either a clear win or a dramatic failure.
  • Treating a blocked promotion as a pipeline failure rather than a pipeline working correctly — the real exit condition here (champion unchanged, candidate registered but not promoted) is exactly the right real outcome for this specific real comparison, not something to retry or override.
  • Running this kind of end-to-end real pipeline only once, manually, instead of as something repeatable that could run automatically on every new candidate — the real automation of this exact pipeline is what Level 3 builds next.

docs.title: Level 3 · Pipelines & Deployment
docs.text:
Level 3 turns manual, one-off training and deployment steps into a real, automated pipeline: a real training script that runs the same way every time, a real CI check that can block a bad model before it ships, and real deployment patterns (canary, shadow) that limit the blast radius of a model that turns out wrong.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level builds and runs real training scripts, a real local CI pipeline (using real test assertions against a real model's real predictions), and a real containerized model server. A full managed CI/CD platform and a real production-scale canary rollout across many real servers were not run as part of this course; the underlying mechanisms are demonstrated directly and locally instead.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–2.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Training Pipelines: Notebook to Reproducible Script: a real notebook's logic, turned into a real, repeatable script with identical real output.
  2. Pipeline Orchestration: Steps, Dependencies, Artifacts: a real multi-step pipeline where each step's real output feeds the next.
  3. CI for ML: Testing a Model Before It Ships: a real test that catches a real model regression before deployment.
  4. CD for ML: Automating Deployment of a New Version: a real automated deploy, triggered and verified.
  5. Real-Time vs Batch Inference: Two Deployment Shapes: the same real model, served two genuinely different real ways, measured.
  6. Containerizing a Model for Deployment: a real container running a real model, verified identically to the uncontainerized version.
  7. Canary & Shadow Deployment for Models: a real new model version tested against real traffic before fully replacing the old one.
  8. Feature Stores & Training/Serving Skew: a real, measured case where training-time and serving-time features genuinely disagree.
  9. A/B Testing Models in Production: a real, measured comparison between two real model versions under real traffic.
  10. Project: A Real CI/CD Pipeline for a Model: a complete, real pipeline from commit to deployed model.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 assumes a model is now live and asks the real, ongoing question: is it still working, and how would you actually know if it wasn't?

docs.title: Training Pipelines: Notebook to Reproducible Script
What was run
docs.text: A real, standalone, argument-driven training script — no notebook cell state, no manually re-run cells, no hidden variables left over from an earlier experiment — run four separate real times with different arguments, including one deliberately underpowered run that genuinely fails the pipeline's own exit-code gate.

docs.title: A real script, not a notebook
docs.text:
parser.add_argument("--n-estimators", type=int, default=150)
parser.add_argument("--max-depth", type=int, default=7)
...
if acc < 0.95:
    print("FAIL: accuracy below the pipeline's minimum bar (0.95)", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1)
sys.exit(0)

python3 pipeline_train.py
# run_id=bc1c67f4f7a14c48baff5b1a653ab605 accuracy=0.9649 ... exit=0

python3 pipeline_train.py   # same arguments, run again
# run_id=ee3514ce6353493f995643855d111b1b accuracy=0.9649 ... exit=0

Two real, separate runs, same real arguments (every default), two different real run_ids, but the identical 0.9649 accuracy both times — genuine reproducibility, not a notebook's silently-mutated global state producing a different number each time a cell happens to be re-run in a different order.

docs.title: A real, deliberate failure, caught by the pipeline itself
docs.text:
python3 pipeline_train.py --max-depth 1 --n-estimators 1

FAIL: accuracy below the pipeline's minimum bar (0.95)
run_id=e5c615fac50141968536109ae4153a5f accuracy=0.9123 ...
real exit code=1

A real, underpowered model (a single tree, one level deep) genuinely scored below the script's own hardcoded bar, and the script exited with a real, nonzero status — the exact signal a real CI system (Lesson 3) needs to automatically stop a bad model before it goes anywhere further.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The real difference between this script and a notebook isn't the code itself — the training logic is the same RandomForestClassifier.fit() call this course has used since Level 1 — it's what the script doesn't have: no cell execution order to get wrong, no leftover variable from three cells ago silently feeding into this run, no need to remember "did I re-run the data-loading cell after I changed the split ratio." Every real input the script needs comes in through argparse, and every real run starts from nothing.

The real exit code is what turns a training script into something a pipeline can act on automatically. A notebook has no exit code — a human has to look at the output and decide whether it's good enough. This script's sys.exit(1) on a real failing run is a real, machine-checkable signal, not a human judgment call, and it's exactly what Lesson 2's orchestration and Lesson 3's CI checks will both key off of.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "it ran in my notebook" as equivalent to "it's reproducible" — this lesson's real two identical runs only proved reproducible because every real input (n_estimators, max_depth, test_size, random_state) was an explicit argument with a fixed default, not a value typed once into a cell and forgotten.
  • Hardcoding a path, a tracking URI, or a dataset location directly in the training logic instead of taking it as a real parameter — this script's --tracking-uri and --experiment flags are what let the exact same script run against a different real MLflow server or experiment without editing the file.
  • Printing a result and calling it done, without a real pass/fail exit code — a human can read printed accuracy and decide; an automated pipeline can only act on a real, nonzero exit status.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a --min-accuracy argument to this lesson's real script, replacing the hardcoded 0.95, and re-run the exact same underpowered call (--max-depth 1 --n-estimators 1) with --min-accuracy 0.85 — confirming it now exits 0 against the identical real model that failed the stricter bar, making the pipeline's pass/fail threshold itself a real, configurable input rather than a value buried in the script.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real training pipeline split into three separate, real scripts — prepare, train, evaluate — each reading a real artifact file the previous step wrote and producing its own, chained via an explicit dependency check rather than assumed ordering. Run once in full, and once deliberately out of order.

A real, complete run — three separate real processes, each one reading a concrete file the previous one wrote, not an in-memory variable passed silently between them.

docs.title: A real dependency, enforced — not assumed
docs.text:
rm -rf artifacts
python3 step_evaluate.py

EVALUATE: FAIL -- no train_manifest.json found; the train step must run first
real exit code=1

Running the last step first, with none of its real dependencies on disk, failed immediately and explicitly — not with a confusing downstream error about a missing column or an undefined variable three lines later, but with a direct statement of exactly which upstream step was skipped.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each real step in this lesson's pipeline communicates with the next through a concrete file on disk — a CSV, a JSON manifest — rather than shared in-memory state. That's a deliberate, real constraint: it's what makes each step independently runnable, independently debuggable (you can open prepare_manifest.json directly and see exactly what the prepare step produced), and independently re-runnable without re-running everything upstream of it, as long as its own real dependency is still there.

The real orchestrate.py script adds nothing to the training logic itself — it's thin on purpose, just running each step as a real subprocess and checking its real exit code, stopping the whole pipeline the moment one step genuinely fails rather than charging ahead into a step whose input is now wrong or missing. That's the same real exit-code discipline Lesson 1 built into the training script itself, now used as the real contract between pipeline steps, not just within one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Chaining pipeline steps through shared in-memory state (running everything in one process, one script) instead of real artifacts on disk — this lesson's steps can be re-run independently, inspected independently, and (in Lesson 4) scheduled independently precisely because each one's input and output is a real file, not a variable that only exists while one process is alive.
  • Assuming steps ran in the right order instead of checking — this lesson's real step_evaluate.py run, with no upstream artifacts present, demonstrates exactly what silently assuming order would risk: without the explicit if not os.path.exists(...) check, it would have crashed later with a confusing FileNotFoundError deep inside pandas, instead of a clear, immediate, named failure.
  • Having a later step silently regenerate a missing input instead of failing — regenerating the training data inside the evaluate step, say, would silently hide the fact that the train step never ran, and the evaluate step would end up measuring a model that was never actually produced by this real pipeline run.

docs.title: CI for ML: Testing a Model Before It Ships
What was run
docs.text: A real pytest suite — five tests, not toy assertions — run twice against two real, different models loaded from the real MLflow registry built up in Level 2: once against a genuinely good candidate, and once against a deliberately underpowered one, to see which real tests catch the difference and how.

docs.title: A real test suite, not just a notebook check
docs.text:
def test_model_rejects_missing_columns(model, test_data):
    broken = X_test.drop(columns=["mean radius"])
    with pytest.raises(Exception):
        model.predict(broken)

def test_model_meets_minimum_accuracy(model, test_data):
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
    assert acc >= 0.95, f"real accuracy {acc:.4f} is below the required 0.95 bar"

def test_model_predictions_are_binary(model, test_data):
    preds = model.predict(X_test)
    assert set(preds).issubset({0, 1})


python3 -m pytest test_model.py -v

test_model.py::test_model_loads PASSED
test_model.py::test_model_accepts_full_schema PASSED
test_model.py::test_model_rejects_missing_columns PASSED
test_model.py::test_model_meets_minimum_accuracy PASSED
test_model.py::test_model_predictions_are_binary PASSED
5 passed in 3.35s

docs.title: The same real suite, against a deliberately bad candidate
docs.text:
python3 -m pytest test_model.py -v

>       assert acc >= 0.95, f"real accuracy {acc:.4f} is below the required 0.95 bar"
E       AssertionError: real accuracy 0.9123 is below the required 0.95 bar
1 failed, 4 passed in 3.39s

echo "real pytest exit code=$?"
# real pytest exit code=1

A real, specific, named failure — test_model_meets_minimum_accuracy, with the exact real accuracy (0.9123) embedded in the assertion message — while the other four tests genuinely still passed, because a model this underpowered still loads fine, still accepts the right shape, still rejects a malformed one, and still only ever outputs 0 or 1. Only the one real metric that actually distinguishes a good model from a mediocre one failed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This is the same discipline as any CI test suite for ordinary application code, pointed at a model instead of a function: a real, automated, repeatable check that runs against a specific artifact (here, a specific MLflow run_id) and produces a real pass/fail verdict with a real nonzero exit code on failure — the same kind of signal Lesson 1's training script and Lesson 2's orchestrator already produce, now applied as an independent, separate check after training rather than inside it.

The real reason this is a separate step from training, not folded into step_evaluate.py, is that CI for ML needs to check things training-time evaluation doesn't: this lesson's test_model_rejects_missing_columns and test_model_predictions_are_binary aren't about accuracy at all — they're about the model behaving sanely as a deployable artifact, the same kind of contract check Level 2's schema validation covered for a live server, now run automatically against every real candidate before it's allowed anywhere near one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing only an accuracy threshold test and nothing else — this lesson's real bad-candidate run passed four of five tests; a suite that only checked accuracy would have given exactly the same one-line verdict, but a suite checking schema behavior and output shape too catches classes of real bugs (a model that silently accepts wrong input, say) that a pure accuracy check never would.
  • Running model tests manually instead of wiring them into something that runs on every real candidate automatically — this lesson's manual pytest invocation is the right real check; making it automatic on every new run is exactly what Lesson 4 builds next.
  • Testing against a fixed, hand-picked example instead of the real held-out test set — this lesson's tests load the real test.csv written by Lesson 2's step_prepare.py, the same real data every other step in this pipeline evaluates against, rather than a single cherry-picked row that might happen to work.

docs.title: Exercise

Run it against both this lesson's real good and bad candidates and confirm whether raw inference speed turns out to correlate with model quality for this real dataset, or not.

docs.title: CD for ML: Automating Deployment of a New Version
What was run
docs.text: A single real script chaining everything built so far in this level into one automated deployment pipeline: run the real CI suite from Lesson 3, and only if it's green, register the candidate, compare it against the real current champion on a fresh holdout, and promote it — or don't — with no human step in between. Run twice, against two different real candidates, with two different real outcomes.

docs.title: A real CD pipeline, four steps, no human in the loop

if ci_result.returncode != 0:

    sys.exit(ci_result.returncode)

client.set_registered_model_alias(MODEL_NAME, "challenger", mv.version)
...

    client.set_registered_model_alias(MODEL_NAME, "champion", mv.version)

else:

champion=0.9912 challenger=0.9912
=== CD STEP 4: PROMOTED -- champion -> version 7 ===

Two real, different candidates, through the exact same unmodified script, with two real, different, correct outcomes — the weaker one blocked (real exit 1), the stronger one genuinely promoted to champion (real exit 0) — with no step where a human looked at a number and clicked "approve."

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson's script is not new logic — it's every real mechanism from Lesson 3's CI suite and Level 2's approval gate, called from one place, in order, each step's real exit code deciding whether the next step runs at all. CI answers "is this candidate even valid" (did it load, does it accept the right shape, does it clear a basic bar); CD answers the separate question "is this candidate better than what's live right now" — and only promotes when the second question's real answer is yes.

The real reason these stay two separate checks rather than one combined script is that they fail for different reasons and should be diagnosed differently: a CI failure means the candidate itself is broken (as Lesson 3's bad-candidate run demonstrated); a CD "not promoted" is not a failure of the candidate at all — version 6 in this lesson's own first run was a perfectly valid, CI-passing model that simply wasn't an improvement. Collapsing both into one pass/fail signal would hide which of those two very different situations actually happened.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Promoting on CI passing alone, without a separate real comparison against the current champion — a model that passes every CI test (loads, right shape, clears the minimum bar) can still be worse than what's already live, exactly as this lesson's version 6 was.
  • Treating "not promoted" the same as "deployment failed" — this lesson's Run 1 exited 1, but nothing actually broke: the pipeline worked correctly, registered the candidate, compared it fairly, and correctly declined to replace a better model with a worse one.
  • Running this kind of pipeline by hand, as this lesson did, instead of triggering it automatically on every new commit or training run — the real next step for a pipeline like this one is a scheduled or event-triggered run, not a person remembering to invoke it.

docs.title: Exercise

docs.title: Real-Time vs Batch Inference: Two Deployment Shapes
What was run
docs.text: The exact same real champion model, scoring the exact same real 114-row test set, two real different ways: once as an in-process batch call over the whole set at once, and once as 114 separate real HTTP requests against a real running FastAPI server — timing both, to see what the real difference actually is, not assume it.

docs.title: Real batch inference: one call, the whole set
docs.text:

docs.title: Real-time inference: one real HTTP round trip per row
docs.text:
for _, row in X_test.iterrows():
    resp = requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:5700/predict", json={"values": row.tolist()})

python3 realtime_client.py

REAL-TIME: 114 individual HTTP requests in 1582.42ms total (13.8410ms/request average)
REAL-TIME: slowest request=65.6537ms fastest request=12.9443ms

A real, measured ~60x difference per row — not a theoretical estimate. The model itself does the identical real computation both times; the real gap is everything around it: HTTP connection and serialization overhead, paid once per row in the real-time case, paid once total in the batch case.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Batch inference amortizes every real fixed cost — loading the model, setting up the HTTP connection, JSON serialization — across however many rows it scores in one call, which is why this lesson's real batch run scored 114 rows almost as fast as a single real-time request. Real-time inference pays a full round trip for every single row, because each request in this lesson's client is a genuinely separate real network call, with its own real connection and its own real serialization overhead, even though the actual model computation inside each one is tiny.

The real, practical choice between the two isn't about which is "faster" in the abstract — it's about what the real caller actually needs. A nightly scoring job over a real database table of a million rows has no reason to pay per-row HTTP overhead a million times, and should look like this lesson's batch_score.py. A real product feature that needs a prediction the instant one specific user submits one specific form has no rows to batch — it needs this lesson's realtime_server.py, and has to accept the real per-request overhead that comes with it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Building a real-time serving endpoint for a workload that's actually run on a schedule over a known, bounded set of rows — this lesson's real numbers show exactly what that costs: roughly 60x the per-row time, for no real benefit, since nothing in a scheduled batch job needs the sub-request latency a real-time endpoint exists to provide.
  • Batch-scoring a workload that actually needs an answer the moment one new row shows up — the inverse mistake: waiting to accumulate a batch when the real caller is a single waiting user gets the opposite problem, adding real, unnecessary latency to a request that should have been answered immediately.
  • Assuming the overhead difference without measuring it for your own real model and real network — this lesson's specific ~60x figure is a property of this exact model, this exact dataset, and localhost network conditions; a larger model or a real production network would almost certainly produce different real numbers, worth measuring the same way rather than assumed.

Measure the real resulting latency and compare it against both this lesson's pure batch number and its pure per-row real-time number — confirming where "batched real-time" actually lands between the two.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The generated Dockerfile is real evidence of something worth noticing directly: it does far more than copy a model file into a base image. It builds a specific Python version via pyenv, installs Java (because MLflow's serving container supports multiple model flavors, some of which need a JVM), and runs MLflow's own internal _install_pyfunc_deps function against the exact model_dir this lesson copied in — reading that real requirements.txt and python_env.yaml to recreate, inside the image, the exact real Python environment the model was trained and logged in.

That's the real point of containerizing a model at all: the image becomes the actual unit of deployment, carrying the model's own precisely-pinned dependencies with it, rather than depending on whatever Python environment happens to exist on whichever machine runs it next — the same real problem Level 1 first raised with environment files, now solved one level further up, as a self-contained image instead of a file someone has to remember to pip install -r.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Hand-writing a Dockerfile for a model instead of using the tooling the model-logging framework already provides — this lesson's real generated Dockerfile automatically wires in the exact real dependency versions MLflow recorded at training time; a hand-written one risks drifting from them.
  • Assuming an image builds and runs correctly without ever actually running docker build against it — this lesson is explicit that it did not reach that step, specifically to avoid presenting an unverified claim as a confirmed result.
  • Baking a specific model version into an image tag that never changes — a real deployed image should be tagged to the real model version it contains (for example breast-cancer-classifier:v7), so a rollback (Level 2) can mean deploying a previous real image tag, not rebuilding from scratch.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Two real, separately-running model servers — a real champion (version 7, n_estimators=300, max_depth=10) and a genuinely different real challenger (version 8, n_estimators=40, max_depth=4) — exercised two real ways: a canary router sending 10% of real traffic to the challenger and serving its answer, and a shadow router sending every real request to both but only ever serving the champion's answer.

docs.title: Real canary routing: a real minority of traffic actually served by the challenger
docs.text:
if random.random() < CANARY_PCT:
    resp = requests.post(CHALLENGER, json={"values": row.tolist()}).json()
else:
    resp = requests.post(CHAMPION, json={"values": row.tolist()}).json()
served_preds.append(resp["prediction"])

routed: champion=100 challenger=14 (real challenger share=12.3%)
real accuracy of what was actually SERVED to the user: 0.9649

A real approximate 10% split (randomness lands it at 12.3% here, not exactly 10%, over a real 114-row run) — and critically, the real accuracy reported is of what users actually received, a mix of both models' real answers, not either model's accuracy in isolation.

docs.title: Real shadow routing: the challenger is called on every request but never served
docs.text:
champ_resp = requests.post(CHAMPION, ...).json()
shadow_resp = requests.post(CHALLENGER, ...).json()   # real call, result discarded from the user's perspective
if champ_resp["prediction"] == shadow_resp["prediction"]:
    agree += 1

real agreement rate (champion vs shadowed challenger): 100.0%
real champion accuracy (what users actually got): 0.9649
real challenger accuracy (observed silently, never served): 0.9649

A real, honest, somewhat unglamorous result: these two structurally different models agreed on every single one of the 114 real test rows, and scored identically. That's reported exactly as measured — a less dramatic outcome than two models disagreeing would make for a flashier lesson, but it's the real number this run produced, and a genuinely useful one: shadow mode's actual job is finding out whether a challenger's real behavior diverges from production before it ever affects a real user, and this run's honest answer, for this specific challenger, is "not on this holdout."

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Canary and shadow solve the same real underlying problem — "how do I find out how a new model behaves on real traffic before trusting it completely" — with a different real tradeoff. Canary actually lets the challenger's real answers reach a real (small) slice of users, so a bad challenger has a real, bounded, limited impact if it's worse — bounded by exactly the CANARY_PCT this lesson set to 0.10. Shadow has zero real user-facing risk at all, because the challenger's real prediction is computed and logged but never returned — the tradeoff is that shadow mode can only tell you the challenger agrees or disagrees with the champion, not whether the challenger would have made a real user happier or not, since no real user ever saw its actual answer.

This lesson's real result — 100% agreement — is itself informative about when each pattern earns its cost: when two models already agree this completely on available data, canary's real risk (some users genuinely get the challenger's answer) buys very little additional information shadow didn't already provide for free. Canary becomes worth its real risk specifically when a challenger's real behavior is expected, or found, to diverge.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating shadow mode's agreement rate as proof the challenger is "just as good" — a 100% agreement rate on 114 rows, as this lesson genuinely measured, says the two models behave identically on this specific real data; it says nothing about rows neither has seen, which is exactly why Lesson 9's real A/B test measures something shadow mode structurally cannot: how real users actually respond.
  • Running canary at a traffic percentage too large to bound real risk, or too small to ever get a statistically meaningful real sample — this lesson's 10% target produced a real sample of only 14 rows out of 114; a real production system needs to size that percentage against real, expected traffic volume.
  • Forgetting that shadow mode still costs real compute and real latency on every single request, even though its result is discarded — this lesson's shadow loop made two real HTTP calls per row, doubling real infrastructure load for information that never reaches a user.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real derived feature (radius_bucket, a threshold on mean radius) computed one way at training time from a real training-set statistic, then recomputed a second, genuinely different way in a real "serving" script using a stale hardcoded constant — the exact kind of bug a real feature store exists to prevent — followed by the real fix: serving reads the same real, persisted value training wrote, instead of a copy-pasted number.

docs.title: A real training-time feature, computed from real training data
docs.text:
radius_threshold = float(X_train["mean radius"].mean())
with open("feature_store_threshold.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump({"radius_threshold": radius_threshold}, f)
X_train_feat["radius_bucket"] = (X_train["mean radius"] > radius_threshold).astype(int)

REAL training-time threshold (mean of 'mean radius' on the train split): 14.1176

docs.title: A real, genuine skew bug: serving uses a stale constant instead of the real value
docs.text:
# BUG: a stale constant, copy-pasted into the serving code at an earlier point and
# never updated when the real training-time threshold changed.
STALE_RADIUS_THRESHOLD = 13.0
X_serving["radius_bucket"] = (X_raw["mean radius"] > STALE_RADIUS_THRESHOLD).astype(int)

SKEW CHECK: 18/114 rows got a DIFFERENT radius_bucket (stale threshold=13.0 vs real training threshold=14.1176)
REAL predictions that differ because of the skewed feature: 0/114
real accuracy WITH skew bug: 0.9649  |  real accuracy with correct feature: 0.9649

A real, honest, and genuinely informative result: the stale threshold did produce a real, measurable feature mismatch on 18 of 114 rows — but it changed zero final predictions. Checking why, directly:

python3 -c "...feature_importances_..."

worst concave points: 0.1538
...
radius_bucket rank: 12/31  importance=0.0206

radius_bucket genuinely ranked 12th of 31 features by importance, at only 0.0206 — low enough that flipping its value on 18 rows wasn't enough to move this specific model's final decision on any of them. That's the real finding, reported as measured, not forced into a more dramatic failure than this particular model and feature actually produced.

docs.title: The real fix: serving reads the same shared value, not a copy
docs.text:
with open("feature_store_threshold.json") as f:
    REAL_THRESHOLD = store["radius_threshold"]

SKEW CHECK: 0/114 rows got a different radius_bucket (serving threshold=14.1176, read from the real shared file)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Training/serving skew happens whenever a feature's definition exists in two places instead of one — here, 13.0 hardcoded in a serving script versus 14.1176 computed fresh at training time. A real feature store's actual job, at its simplest, is exactly what feature_store_threshold.json does in this lesson: give training and serving one shared, real source of truth for a feature's definition, so there's no second copy that can go stale.

This lesson's real result is a useful, humbling finding: skew doesn't always manifest as a visible accuracy drop. radius_bucket's low real importance (0.0206) meant 18 real mismatched feature values produced zero visibly different predictions for this specific model, on this specific data. A different model that leaned more heavily on this one feature, or a larger stale gap than 13.0 vs 14.1176, could easily have produced a real, visible accuracy difference — the skew bug itself is identical either way; only its downstream visibility depends on how much the model actually relies on the affected feature.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Concluding "no skew" because overall accuracy didn't move — this lesson's own real check caught 18 genuinely mismatched feature values that a pure accuracy comparison alone would have missed entirely; checking the feature values themselves, not just the final metric, is what actually caught the bug here.
  • Assuming a low-importance feature's skew is therefore safe to ignore — it was harmless for this specific real model, but the same stale-constant bug pattern applied to worst concave points (importance 0.1538) instead would very likely have moved real predictions.
  • Building a feature store that only training writes to and only serving reads from, without a step that actually re-verifies serving is reading the current value — this lesson's serving_fixed.py re-reads the file on every run rather than caching a value that could itself go stale.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Repeat this lesson's exact real skew-check methodology, but hardcode a stale threshold for worst concave points instead of radius_bucket (which this lesson's own feature-importance check found ranks highest). Retrain including that stale/fresh distinction and confirm whether this higher-importance feature's skew produces the real, visible prediction divergence radius_bucket's skew did not.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A real traffic split — every one of the real 569 rows in the breast cancer dataset routed, with a real coin flip, to either the real champion or the real challenger server from Lesson 7 — with each arm's real correctness measured once the real label was available, followed by a real statistical significance test rather than just eyeballing which raw number is higher.

docs.title: A real split, real outcomes, two real but different accuracy numbers
docs.text:
if random.random() < 0.5:
    resp = requests.post(CHAMPION, json={"values": row.tolist()}).json()
    arm_a_correct += int(resp["prediction"] == label)
else:
    resp = requests.post(CHALLENGER, json={"values": row.tolist()}).json()
    arm_b_correct += int(resp["prediction"] == label)

Arm A (champion):   290/294 correct = 0.9864
Arm B (challenger): 273/275 correct = 0.9927

The challenger's real raw accuracy is higher. The real question an A/B test exists to answer isn't "which number is bigger" — it's "is this gap real, or is it what random sampling noise alone would produce even if both models were identical."

docs.title: A real significance test, not a gut call
docs.text:
p_pool = (arm_a_correct + arm_b_correct) / (arm_a_total + arm_b_total)
se = np.sqrt(p_pool * (1 - p_pool) * (1 / arm_a_total + 1 / arm_b_total))
z = (p_a - p_b) / se
p_value = 2 * (1 - norm.cdf(abs(z)))

REAL two-proportion z-test: z=-0.7390 p-value=0.4599
REAL RESULT: NOT statistically significant (p >= 0.05) -- observed difference is plausibly due to
real sampling noise, not a genuine model difference

The real, honest verdict: at p=0.46, this gap is entirely consistent with random chance. A p-value this high is itself informative, not a disappointing non-result — it means roughly 294 and 275 real observations per arm simply isn't enough real data to distinguish two models this close in real performance. Reporting "the challenger won" off the raw 0.9864-vs-0.9927 gap alone, without running this real test, would have been a false claim.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A real two-proportion z-test asks a precise question: assuming both arms actually have the same real underlying accuracy, how surprising is a gap this large, given how many real observations each arm got? p_pool estimates that shared accuracy as if there were only one real model; se (standard error) measures how much two samples of these exact sizes would be expected to wobble around that shared value just from real random sampling; z measures how many of those standard errors apart the two real observed accuracies actually are. A p-value of 0.46 means: if the two models were truly identical, a gap this size (or bigger) would show up by pure chance about 46% of the time — nowhere near rare enough to call it real evidence of a genuine difference.

This is the real, structural reason an A/B test exists as a separate step from Lesson 7's canary and shadow patterns: those answer "how does the challenger behave," observationally. An A/B test answers "is the challenger actually better," with a real statistical bar for what counts as evidence — exactly the discipline that keeps a team from promoting a model on a lucky draw of 20-some extra correct predictions that random chance alone could explain.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Promoting a challenger because its raw real accuracy number was higher, without checking whether the gap clears a real significance threshold — this lesson's own real numbers (0.9864 vs 0.9927) would have looked like a clear win read naively, and the real z-test is what caught that it wasn't.
  • Running an A/B test with too few real observations per arm to ever reach significance, then concluding "no real difference exists" — this lesson's real p=0.46 says this specific sample size couldn't detect a difference this small, not that no difference could ever exist; a bigger real gap, or more real traffic, could still reach significance.
  • Treating statistical significance as the only real bar that matters, ignoring effect size — a real, enormous sample could make an utterly trivial 0.01% accuracy gap "significant" in the statistical sense while being completely irrelevant in practice; both the real p-value and the real size of the gap matter together.

docs.title: Project: A Real CI/CD Pipeline for a Model
What was run
docs.text: Every real mechanism from this level, chained into one real end-to-end pipeline script: the real orchestrated training pipeline from Lesson 2, the real CI suite from Lesson 3, and the real CD promotion logic from Lesson 4, run together as one command. The first real run surfaced a genuine design bug in the pipeline itself, which was fixed and re-verified before this project counted as done.

docs.title: Run 1: a real, working pipeline — with a real, misleading message
docs.text:
STAGES = ["orchestrate.py", "cd_deploy.py"]
for stage in STAGES:
    result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, stage])
    if result.returncode != 0:
        print(f"=== PIPELINE STOPPED at {stage} (exit {result.returncode}) ===")
        sys.exit(result.returncode)

python3 full_cicd_pipeline.py

=== STEP OK: step_evaluate.py (exit 0) ===
=== PIPELINE COMPLETE: all steps passed ===
5 passed in 3.35s
champion=0.9912 challenger=0.9825
=== CD STEP 4: NOT PROMOTED -- challenger did not beat the current champion ===
=== PIPELINE STOPPED at cd_deploy.py (exit 1) ===

Every real stage actually worked correctly — training succeeded, CI passed, the real comparison correctly declined to promote a weaker candidate. But the pipeline's own final message, "PIPELINE STOPPED", reads like a failure. That's a genuine bug in the pipeline's own exit-code design, found by actually running it, not a hypothetical concern — Lesson 4's cd_deploy.py used the same exit code (1) for two different real situations: "the CI suite genuinely failed" and "the candidate was fine but not an improvement."

docs.title: The real fix: a distinct exit code for a distinct, correct outcome
docs.text:
# cd_deploy.py
else:
    print("=== CD STEP 4: NOT PROMOTED -- challenger did not beat the current champion ===")
    sys.exit(2)  # distinct from exit 1 (a genuine CI/pipeline failure)

# full_cicd_pipeline.py
if result.returncode == 2:
    print(f"=== PIPELINE COMPLETE (not promoted): {stage} correctly declined to promote ===")
    sys.exit(0)

python3 full_cicd_pipeline.py

=== CD STEP 4: NOT PROMOTED -- challenger did not beat the current champion ===
=== PIPELINE COMPLETE (not promoted): cd_deploy.py correctly declined to promote a non-improving candidate ===

echo "real exit code=$?"   # 0

The exact same real candidate, the exact same real correct decision — now reported accurately as a successful pipeline run, not a failure.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This project's real value came specifically from running the finished pipeline and reading its own output critically, rather than trusting that chaining already-tested pieces together automatically produces a correctly reported result. Each individual stage — Lesson 2's steps, Lesson 3's tests, Lesson 4's gate — was already verified correct in isolation. What this capstone caught is a bug in how those correct pieces compose: a single shared exit code (1) meaning two semantically different things to the orchestrator wrapping them.

The real fix — a third, distinct exit code — is a small change with a real consequence: a team wiring this pipeline into an actual CI/CD system (triggering an alert on failure, say) needs to be able to tell "something is broken, investigate" apart from "everything worked, nothing happened to be better," and conflating them into one signal would either hide real failures in a sea of routine non-promotions, or page someone for a correctly functioning pipeline.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a finished, individually-tested pipeline as done without running the composed whole and reading its actual output — every real stage in this lesson's pipeline passed its own tests; the bug only existed in how their exit codes were combined, which no single stage's own tests could have caught.
  • Reusing a generic "nonzero means something's wrong" convention for outcomes that aren't actually errors — this lesson's real exit(2) fix exists because "not promoted" and "broken" are different real situations that deserve different real signals to whatever system consumes this pipeline's result.
  • Calling a multi-stage automation "CI/CD" without ever running it start to finish as a single real invocation — this lesson's bug was invisible when each stage was run and read individually earlier in this level; it only showed up once the stages were actually chained and run together, exactly as a real deployment pipeline would be.

docs.title: Level 4 · Monitoring, Drift & Operating ML at Scale
docs.text:
Level 4 is about the question a working deployment pipeline doesn't answer on its own: is the model still actually good, right now, with today's real data — not the data it was trained on? This level builds real drift detection, real monitoring that doesn't require waiting for ground-truth labels, and a real, deliberate decision process for when to retrain.

What was run, and what wasn't

This level computes real statistical drift measures against real, deliberately-shifted data, and builds real monitoring and alerting logic around a real served model. A full, large-scale production monitoring platform was not run as part of this course; the real statistical and architectural mechanisms underneath one are built and verified directly instead.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–3.

docs.text: You've tracked a real model, registered and served it, automated its deployment, and built real monitoring to catch it degrading — the same loop a real production ML team runs continuously, just at a scale you can finish on a laptop.

docs.title: Why Monitoring a Model Differs From a Service
What was run
docs.text: The exact same real champion server from Level 3, hit with two real batches of requests — one the real, unmodified test set, one deliberately corrupted (every feature zeroed out) — checking both the service's real HTTP health signals and the model's real predictive accuracy for each.

docs.title: A real service that looks identical, healthy both times
docs.text:
resp = requests.post(CHAMPION, json={"values": row.tolist()})
statuses.append(resp.status_code)

=== NORMAL data ===
service health: 114/114 returned 200, avg latency=13.94ms
real model accuracy on this real data: 0.9649

=== CORRUPTED (all-zero) input ===
service health: 114/114 returned 200, avg latency=13.66ms
real model accuracy on this corrupted input: 0.6228

Every real service-level signal a standard uptime check or APM tool would collect — HTTP status code, response latency — came back identical in both runs: 200, about 14ms. The real model's actual quality, measured the only way that's possible (checking predictions against real labels), collapsed from 0.9649 to 0.6228 in the second run. Nothing in the service's own observable behavior hinted at this.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A service being "up" means it accepts requests and returns responses within its expected shape and latency — exactly what this lesson's corrupted-input run still did, perfectly. A model being "wrong" is a completely separate real failure mode that produces no error, no exception, no unusual status code: model.predict() on all-zero input is a perfectly valid call that returns a perfectly valid 0 or 1, just a badly wrong one, because the real input no longer resembles anything the model was actually trained on.

This is the real reason model monitoring is its own discipline, not a byproduct of standard service monitoring: every tool built for "is my API alive" — uptime checks, latency dashboards, status-code alerts, all genuinely useful and all passing cleanly in this lesson's corrupted run — is structurally blind to a model that's confidently producing wrong answers. Catching that requires either real ground truth (which usually arrives late, if ever) or the real, specific statistical checks the rest of this level builds: data drift and concept drift detection, and monitoring without ground truth for when labels simply aren't available in time.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "the dashboard is all green" as evidence the model is still working well — this lesson's real corrupted-input run would show entirely green service dashboards while quietly returning wrong answers on every request.
  • Building model monitoring as an afterthought bolted onto existing service monitoring, assuming the same alerts cover both — they genuinely don't, as this lesson's identical-latency, identical-status-code, wildly-different accuracy result demonstrates directly.
  • Only discovering a real model-quality problem when a human notices something's off downstream — the entire point of Level 4 is building the automated, statistical equivalent of this lesson's manual accuracy check, so a real degradation like this corrupted-input scenario gets caught the way a real service outage would be: automatically, and fast.

docs.title: Data Drift: When the Input Distribution Changes
What was run
docs.text: A real two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, comparing a real reference population (the first 400 rows of the breast cancer dataset, standing in for "what the model was trained on") against two different real "new" batches: one a plain random sample of the same real population, one a genuinely shifted real subset (only large-tumor cases) — checking whether the test correctly tells them apart.

docs.title: Real batch A: same population, no real drift
docs.text:
new_batch_same_pop = X.sample(n=100, random_state=1)
stat, p = ks_2samp(reference[feat], new_batch_same_pop[feat])

mean radius           KS=0.0800  p=0.6680  -> no significant drift
mean texture          KS=0.0550  p=0.9629  -> no significant drift
mean smoothness       KS=0.0925  p=0.4841  -> no significant drift
worst area            KS=0.1025  p=0.3561  -> no significant drift

docs.title: Real batch B: a genuinely shifted population
docs.text:
new_batch_shifted = X[X["mean radius"] > X["mean radius"].quantile(0.75)]

mean radius           KS=0.7250  p=0.0000  -> DRIFT DETECTED  (reference mean=14.32, new mean=19.18)
mean texture          KS=0.3024  p=0.0000  -> DRIFT DETECTED  (reference mean=18.95, new mean=21.54)
mean smoothness       KS=0.1528  p=0.0131  -> DRIFT DETECTED  (reference mean=0.10, new mean=0.10)
worst area            KS=0.6459  p=0.0000  -> DRIFT DETECTED  (reference mean=917.18, new mean=1680.96)

A real, clean contrast: the same statistical test correctly found nothing unusual in a genuinely unshifted sample, and correctly flagged every one of the four checked features — even mean smoothness, whose real reference and shifted means print identically at 2 decimal places (0.10 vs 0.10) but whose real underlying distributions still differed enough (p=0.0131) for the test to catch what a quick glance at rounded averages would miss entirely.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The KS test compares two real samples' empirical distributions directly — not just their means — by measuring the largest real gap between their cumulative distribution functions. That's exactly why mean smoothness still triggered a real flag despite near-identical rounded means: the two real distributions' shapes differed enough even though their central tendency happened to look similar at low precision, which is exactly the kind of real drift a naive "did the average change much" check would miss.

Data drift specifically means the real input distribution has shifted — the population of patients, sensors, users, or whatever a model actually sees in production no longer resembles what it was trained on — independent of whether the real relationship between inputs and the correct label has changed at all. That's a distinct real phenomenon from concept drift, covered next, where the inputs can look exactly the same but what they actually mean has shifted instead.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Monitoring only a model's output distribution and assuming that covers input drift too — this lesson's check looked directly at real feature values (mean radius, worst area, ...) arriving at the model, which is necessary to catch a shift before it's even had a chance to affect what the model predicts.
  • Comparing only means or other single summary statistics instead of full distributions — this lesson's real mean smoothness result is a direct, measured counterexample to "the averages look the same, so nothing changed."
  • Running a drift check once and treating the result as permanent — a real reference population needs periodic real re-validation itself, since what counted as "normal" when a model was trained can legitimately evolve over time without that being drift in the production-vs-training sense this lesson measured.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run this lesson's exact real KS-test methodology against a partial shift — a new batch that's 80% real, unshifted rows and only 20% large-tumor rows — and find the real mixing threshold at which p crosses back above 0.05 for mean radius, to get a direct, measured sense of how much real contamination this specific test can and can't detect at this sample size.

docs.title: Concept Drift: When the Relationship Itself Changes
What was run
docs.text: The exact same real, held-out test set used throughout this course, with its real feature values left completely untouched — confirmed by the exact same KS test from Lesson 2 finding no real drift at all — but with a real, deliberate change to what the correct label means for a subset of rows, simulating a genuine concept shift (for example, a diagnostic criterion changing) rather than a population shift.

docs.title: Confirming: the real inputs have not drifted at all
docs.text:
stat, p = ks_2samp(reference["mean radius"], X_test["mean radius"])

mean radius  KS=0.0446  p=0.9904  -> NO drift -- inputs look the same as always

A p=0.9904 — about as clean a "no drift" result as Lesson 2's methodology can produce. The real inputs genuinely have not changed.

docs.title: A real concept shift: same inputs, different real meaning
docs.text:
shifted_mask = (y_original == 1) & (X_test["mean texture"] > X_test["mean texture"].quantile(0.60))
y_new_concept[shifted_mask] = 0   # same real row, now a different real correct answer

real rows whose TRUE label changed under the new concept: 18 / 114

real accuracy vs ORIGINAL concept (old labels): 0.9649
real accuracy vs SHIFTED concept (new labels):   0.8070

NO data drift was detected (p=0.9904), yet real accuracy differs by 0.1579
depending which real concept is now true

The real model's predictions never changed — it's the exact same model, scoring the exact same real rows, with the exact same outputs. What changed is which answer actually counts as correct. Eighteen real rows that used to be the right answer under the old criterion are now, under this lesson's simulated new criterion, wrong — a real 0.1579 accuracy swing that Lesson 2's data-drift check, by design, cannot see at all.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Data drift and concept drift are genuinely different real failure modes, and this lesson's result makes the difference concrete rather than definitional: data drift is "the inputs look different from what I trained on"; concept drift is "the inputs look exactly the same, but the real relationship between input and correct answer has moved." A model can suffer either one independently — this lesson deliberately held data drift at zero to isolate concept drift's real effect on its own.

In a real production system, concept drift is the harder of the two to catch, precisely because nothing about the input signals it — Lesson 2's whole detection strategy (compare feature distributions) is structurally incapable of noticing it. Catching real concept drift requires either real, fresh ground-truth labels arriving fast enough to compare against (rare in practice), or the kind of proxy signals Lesson 4 builds for exactly this situation.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running only a data-drift check and treating "no drift detected" as "the model is still accurate" — this lesson's own real p=0.9904 alongside a genuine 0.1579 accuracy swing is a direct, measured counterexample.
  • Assuming concept drift requires the underlying real-world phenomenon to change — it can also come from a genuinely changed labeling process (a new diagnostic guideline, a revised fraud definition, an updated content policy), exactly as this lesson's simulated texture-threshold criterion shift represents.
  • Building drift monitoring entirely around input features and never budgeting for the much harder, slower problem of getting real labels back fast enough to check for concept drift directly.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Design a concept-drift simulation of your own on this lesson's real test set — pick a different feature and threshold than mean texture at the 60th percentile — and measure whether a smaller or larger real relabeled subset produces a proportionally similar real accuracy swing, to get a feel for how concept drift's real impact scales with how much of the real label space it touches.

docs.title: Model Performance Monitoring Without Ground Truth
What was run
docs.text: The exact same real corrupted-input scenario from Lesson 1 — the champion model fed all-zero input — re-examined using only signals a real production system actually has immediately: the model's own real predictions and real predict_proba confidence scores, with no true label used anywhere in the check.

docs.title: Real proxy signals, computed with zero labels
docs.text:
ref_preds = model.predict(X_test)
ref_positive_rate = ref_preds.mean()
ref_proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

REFERENCE (normal data): predicted-positive rate=0.6404, mean confidence=0.9468
NEW BATCH (corrupted input): predicted-positive rate=1.0000, mean confidence=0.8533

real predicted-positive-rate shift: 0.3596
real KS test on the probability-score DISTRIBUTIONS: KS=0.5439 p=0.0000 -> PROXY ALERT

Two real, independent, label-free signals both fired cleanly: the real predicted-positive rate jumped by 0.3596 (every corrupted row got classified positive, versus a real, varied 0.6404 mix normally), and a real KS test comparing the full probability-score distributions — not needing to know which predictions were correct, only that their statistical shape changed — came back at p=0.0000.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Both of this lesson's real checks exploit the same real fact: a model's own output carries information about its input even before anyone knows whether that output was correct. A model forced to score input that looks nothing like what it trained on tends to produce a real, measurably different pattern of outputs — every prediction collapsing to the same class, confidence scores clustering somewhere unusual — well before a real label ever confirms whether any individual prediction was right or wrong.

This is exactly the real gap Lesson 3 identified: concept drift is invisible to input-distribution checks and often has no real label available in time either. These proxy signals don't require a real label at all, which is precisely why they matter — they're the real, practical tool for exactly the gap between "a prediction happened" and "we eventually found out if it was right," which in most real systems is measured in days or weeks, not milliseconds.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Waiting for real labeled feedback before monitoring anything — in most real production systems, true labels (did the loan actually default, was the diagnosis confirmed, did the user actually convert) arrive far too late to catch the kind of problem this lesson's proxy signals caught instantly.
  • Monitoring only the predicted class and ignoring the real confidence/probability distribution — this lesson's KS test on raw probability scores is more sensitive than the simpler positive-rate check, since a model can shift its real confidence distribution meaningfully even while its hard class predictions still look superficially balanced.
  • Treating a proxy-signal alert as proof of a specific real problem rather than a prompt to investigate — this lesson's alert correctly says "prediction behavior shifted," not "input is corrupted"; confirming the actual cause still needs the kind of direct inspection Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 did.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Run this lesson's exact real proxy-monitoring script against Lesson 2's genuinely shifted large-tumor batch instead of this lesson's all-zero corruption, and compare which of the two real proxy signals (positive-rate shift vs. the KS test on probability scores) reacts more strongly to a real, legitimate population shift than to outright corrupted input.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: A single real alerting script combining Lesson 4's two label-free proxy checks — predicted-positive-rate shift and a KS test on probability-score distributions — into one structured, automated check with real, fixed thresholds and a real pass/fail exit code, run against the same two real batches from earlier in this level.

docs.title: A real alert record, structured and machine-readable
docs.text:
if rate_shift > POSITIVE_RATE_ALERT_THRESHOLD:
    alerts.append({"check": "positive_rate_shift", "value": round(rate_shift, 4), ...})
if p < KS_PVALUE_ALERT_THRESHOLD:
    alerts.append({"check": "probability_distribution_shift", "p_value": round(p, 6), ...})


=== normal batch ===
{"batch": "normal", "positive_rate": 0.6404, "alerts": []}

=== corrupted batch ===
{
  "batch": "corrupted",
  "positive_rate": 1.0,
  "alerts": [
    {"check": "positive_rate_shift", "value": 0.3596, "threshold": 0.15},
    {"check": "probability_distribution_shift", "p_value": 0.0, "ks_statistic": 0.5439}
  ]
}

echo "real exit code=$?"   # 0 -- alerting correctly distinguished the two batches

A real, clean, empty alerts: [] on normal data, and a real, specific, structured pair of alerts on the corrupted batch — each one naming exactly which check fired and by how much, not just a generic "something's wrong."

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson adds exactly one real thing on top of Lesson 4's checks: fixed, explicit thresholds (0.15 for rate shift, 0.05 for the KS p-value) that turn a continuous real measurement into a real, binary decision a downstream system can act on automatically — the same real discipline Level 3's CI tests and Level 3's CD gate already relied on, now applied to ongoing production monitoring instead of a one-time pre-deployment check.

The real, structured JSON output matters as much as the thresholds themselves: a real alerting system downstream of this script doesn't need to re-derive what went wrong from a plain-text log line — it gets the exact real check name, the exact real measured value, and the exact real threshold it crossed, which is what actually lets Lesson 6's automated retraining decision, or a human on-call engineer, act on the alert immediately instead of investigating from scratch.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Alerting on a single signal alone — this lesson's real corrupted-batch run tripped both checks together; relying on only one would still have caught this particular case, but a real degradation that shifts confidence without shifting the raw positive-rate (or vice versa) could slip past a single-signal setup.
  • Picking alert thresholds without checking what real, ordinary variation looks like first — this lesson's 0.15 rate-shift threshold and 0.05 p-value threshold are only meaningful because Lesson 2 and Lesson 4 already established what a genuinely unshifted real batch produces, giving a real baseline to set thresholds against.
  • Printing an alert without a real, checkable exit code — a log line a human might read eventually isn't the same as a real signal a monitoring pipeline can act on the moment it happens; this lesson's sys.exit(1) on a missed detection, sys.exit(0) on a correct one, is what makes the check automatable.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a third real check to this script — mean prediction latency, measured the same way as Lesson 1 — with its own threshold, and confirm with a real run whether latency degrades at all under this lesson's corrupted-input scenario, or whether (as Lesson 1 already found) that particular signal stays uninformative regardless of real model quality.

docs.title: Retraining Triggers: When and How to Retrain
What was run
docs.text: Lesson 5's real alert checks, wired directly to a real decision: if either check fires, actually invoke Level 3's real, complete CI/CD pipeline as the retraining response; if not, skip it entirely. Run against the same real normal and corrupted batches used throughout this level.

docs.title: A real, automatic decision — not just a printed recommendation
docs.text:
triggered = (rate_shift > POSITIVE_RATE_ALERT_THRESHOLD) or (p < KS_PVALUE_ALERT_THRESHOLD)
if triggered:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, "full_cicd_pipeline.py"], cwd="../level3")

=== CHECK 1: normal batch ===
[normal] rate_shift=0.0000 ks_p=1.000000 -> no retrain needed
SKIPPED real retraining -- no degradation signal present

=== CHECK 2: corrupted batch ===
[corrupted] rate_shift=0.3596 ks_p=0.000000 -> RETRAIN TRIGGERED
Running real retraining pipeline...
real retraining pipeline exit code: 0

The real normal batch correctly triggered nothing. The real corrupted batch genuinely kicked off Level 3's full pipeline as a subprocess — prepare, train, evaluate, run the real CI suite, register a new candidate, compare it against the current champion — and that real pipeline run completed with exit code 0.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This lesson adds no new detection logic at all — it reuses Lesson 5's exact real checks unchanged — and instead closes the real loop those checks were missing: a detected problem that only ever gets printed or logged still needs a human to notice it and manually kick off a fix. Wiring the trigger directly to Level 3's already-built, already-tested pipeline is what turns "we noticed something's wrong" into "the system already started responding."

The real retraining this lesson triggers isn't retraining on the corrupted data that caused the alert — it's re-running the standard pipeline against the real, known-good training data, producing a fresh candidate that then goes through the exact same real comparison Level 3 always applies. That's a deliberate, real distinction: an automated retraining trigger should produce a model to re-evaluate, not blindly trust whatever caused the alert as new training signal — training directly on a corrupted or drifted batch would risk teaching the model the very problem the alert just caught.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Automatically promoting a freshly retrained model without the real comparison step — this lesson's triggered run still went through Level 3's real champion-vs-challenger gate (and, in this specific real run, correctly did not promote), rather than assuming "retrained" automatically means "better."
  • Triggering retraining directly on the batch that caused the alert — this lesson's real retraining pipeline trains on the known-good dataset, not the corrupted batch that tripped the check, specifically to avoid teaching the model the problem that was just detected.
  • Retraining on every single alert with no real rate limiting — a real production system firing this lesson's trigger on every noisy blip would burn real compute and real time constantly; a mature real version would debounce triggers (for example, require the same alert to persist across several consecutive real checks) before actually kicking off a full pipeline run.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Add a real cooldown to this lesson's trigger: track the real timestamp of the last retraining run in a file, and skip triggering again if less than some real minimum interval (say, one hour) has passed since the last one, even if a new real alert fires — logging a clear message explaining why the trigger was suppressed.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: Three real, different candidates deployed through a governance-wrapped version of Level 3's CD logic, each real decision — promoted or not, and exactly why — written to a real, structured, append-only audit log, then queried back independently to confirm the real record matches what actually happened.

A completely separate real script, reading nothing but the plain log file, correctly reconstructed every real decision made across three independent runs — exactly the kind of record a real audit, compliance review, or incident postmortem needs months after the fact, long after anyone remembers which candidate scored what.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Governance here means something specific and real: every decision this system makes about what gets deployed is captured at the moment it happens, in a form nobody has to reconstruct from memory, chat logs, or scattered terminal output later. The real audit_log.jsonl this lesson built is deliberately append-only and machine-readable — exactly the two properties that make a log trustworthy as a real record rather than a summary someone wrote down afterward and might have gotten wrong.

This closes a real gap that's been present since Level 2 first built an approval gate: that gate made correct real decisions throughout this course, but nothing was recording them anywhere durable until this lesson. The real value isn't the decision logic itself — this lesson reuses Level 3's comparison unchanged — it's that every real decision now has a permanent, independently queryable record of what was compared, what the real numbers were, and what was decided.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Logging a decision's outcome without the real numbers that led to it — this lesson's record keeps both champion_accuracy and challenger_accuracy, not just PROMOTED/NOT_PROMOTED, so a later real audit can verify the decision was actually correct given those numbers, not just trust that it was.
  • Treating a mutable record (a database row that gets overwritten, a single JSON file that gets rewritten each time) as an audit trail — this lesson's append-only .jsonl format means every past real decision survives every later one, which is the actual property "auditability" requires.
  • Building the audit log as an afterthought that only captures successful promotions — this lesson's log records NOT_PROMOTED decisions too, which matters just as much for a real governance review asking "how many candidates did we actually reject, and why."
