docs.title: Cost & Latency Tradeoffs in Model Serving
What was run
docs.text: Four real RandomForestClassifier configurations — from a genuinely tiny model to a genuinely large one — each real one trained, evaluated for real accuracy, and timed for real per-1000-row prediction latency, logged to MLflow, to see exactly what a bigger real model actually buys over a smaller one.

docs.title: Four real configurations, both metrics measured together
docs.text:
CONFIGS = [("tiny", 5, 3), ("small", 25, 5), ("medium", 100, 7), ("large", 500, 15)]
X_timed = pd.concat([X_test] * 10, ignore_index=True).iloc[:1000]
start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(5):
    model.predict(X_timed)
elapsed_per_1k = (time.perf_counter() - start) / 5 * 1000

config    n_est  depth   accuracy   latency/1k rows (ms)
tiny          5      3     0.9561                   0.79
small        25      5     0.9649                   1.95
medium      100      7     0.9649                   5.34
large       500     15     0.9649                  25.53

docs.title: A real, measured diminishing return
docs.text:
small   : +0.0088 accuracy for +1.16ms/1k-rows real latency
medium  : +0.0088 accuracy for +4.55ms/1k-rows real latency
large   : +0.0088 accuracy for +24.74ms/1k-rows real latency

A real, striking pattern: every one of the three larger configurations bought the exact same real accuracy improvement over the tiny baseline (+0.0088) — small, medium, and large all landed on identical real test accuracy (0.9649) — while paying a sharply increasing real latency cost to get there. Past small, this specific real dataset simply had nothing further for a bigger model to find; the extra real capacity in medium and large bought zero additional real accuracy, only more real latency.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Cost and latency in model serving scale with real model complexity — more trees, deeper trees, more real computation per prediction — but real accuracy doesn't necessarily scale alongside it. This lesson's numbers are a direct, measured illustration of a genuinely common real pattern: a dataset or problem has a real ceiling on how much a given model family can learn from it, and once a real model is complex enough to reach that ceiling, more complexity only adds real cost without adding real value.

The real, practical conclusion this lesson's own numbers support isn't "bigger is better" or "smaller is always fine" — it's that the real tradeoff has to be measured, per problem, rather than assumed. For this specific real dataset, small (25 trees, depth 5) was the genuinely efficient choice: it captured all the real accuracy large did, at roughly 1/13th the real latency. A different, harder real dataset might show a genuinely different curve, with large continuing to earn its real cost well past where this one plateaued.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Choosing model size based on accuracy alone, without ever measuring the real latency or compute cost that size actually buys — this lesson's own numbers show three configurations tied on accuracy while differing by more than 20x in real latency.
  • Assuming a bigger, more complex model will always be at least as accurate as a smaller one — on a real, harder, noisier problem than this one, a model that's too large can genuinely overfit and score worse on real held-out data than a smaller one, not just cost more.
  • Measuring latency once, at low batch sizes, and extrapolating — this lesson measured over a real, repeated 1000-row batch specifically to get a stable number; a single-row timing measurement is dominated by one-off overhead and would not reflect real sustained throughput cost.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text: Re-run this lesson's exact real sweep with a fifth configuration between tiny and small (try n_estimators=15, max_depth=4) to find, by direct real measurement rather than guessing, roughly where this specific real dataset's accuracy ceiling actually starts — the real point past which added model size stops paying for itself.

docs.title: What was run
docs.text: No new code — this lesson is a direct review of real anti-patterns this exact course genuinely ran into while being built, each one documented honestly in its own lesson at the time it happened, not invented after the fact to illustrate a point.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 1: Trusting a serialization format without checking what it actually requires
docs.text: Level 1, Lesson 1 hit a real skops.io.exceptions.UntrustedTypesFoundException the first time mlflow.sklearn.log_model() was ever called in this course, because MLflow 3.x's default skops format refuses to deserialize sklearn.tree._tree.Tree without explicit permission. The fix (skops_trusted_types=[...]) had to be discovered by reading the real exception, not assumed in advance.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 2: Assuming a model is missing because it's not where you expect
docs.text: The same lesson later found real runs whose artifacts appeared to be missing entirely — checked against the old mlruns/<run_id>/artifacts/model/ path — when MLflow 3.x's real Logged Models architecture had actually stored them at a completely different, new real location (mlruns/<exp>/models/m-<id>/artifacts/) all along.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 3: Building on an API that's already printing its own deprecation warning
docs.text: Level 2, Lesson 2 used the classic transition_model_version_stage() call, which worked, but printed a real FutureWarning stating it's deprecated since MLflow 2.9.0. The lesson pivoted its real teaching content to aliases rather than building further on a mechanism already flagged for removal.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 4: Deploying a model with no signature at all
docs.text: Level 2, Lesson 8 found the real, live, already-promoted champion model had no signature (get_input_schema() returned None) because the script that trained it never called infer_signature() — a real gap that had passed through a real approval gate undetected.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 5: Letting one exit code mean two different things
docs.text: Level 3, Lesson 10's first real end-to-end run printed "PIPELINE STOPPED" for a run that had actually succeeded — a correctly-declined, non-improving promotion — because cd_deploy.py used the same exit code (1) for "genuinely broken" and "correctly not promoted."

docs.title: Anti-pattern 6: A stale constant quietly diverging from the real source of truth
docs.text: Level 3, Lesson 8 hardcoded a serving-side threshold (13.0) that had genuinely gone stale against the real training-time value (14.1176) — a real, measurable feature-value mismatch on 18 of 114 rows, caught only by checking feature values directly, not by watching accuracy alone.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 7: Reading internal exceptions as if they were intentional API responses
docs.text: Level 2, Lesson 7 found the raw mlflow models serve endpoint's real response to a malformed request was a scikit-learn internal ValueError with a full stack trace embedded in the JSON body — a real, leaky error response, in contrast to the clean, structured 400 Lesson 8's dedicated validation layer produced for the identical malformed input.

docs.title: Anti-pattern 8: Mistaking "no data drift" for "the model is still fine"
docs.text: Level 4, Lesson 3 measured a real p=0.9904 on a KS drift test — strong evidence of no input drift at all — on the exact same real batch where a simulated concept shift genuinely dropped accuracy by 0.1579. Each anti-pattern on this list is a real, specific failure mode; this one is the general shape nearly all of them share: a signal that looks clean is not the same as a system that's actually fine.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: What ties every real item on this list together is the same real discipline this entire course has tried to model directly: none of these were caught by assuming the tooling, the framework, or a previous lesson's code was correct. Every one was caught by actually running something and reading its real output critically — an exception message, a warning, a None where a value was expected, a confusing status message, a feature value that didn't match. The anti-pattern isn't any single mistake on this list; it's trusting a system's surface signal (ran without crashing, returned 200, printed a seemingly reasonable message) over directly verifying what it actually did.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading this list as "things that could theoretically go wrong" rather than what it actually is: a real, dated incident log from one specific course build, each entry traceable to the exact lesson where it happened and was fixed in place.
  • Assuming a framework this mature (MLflow, scikit-learn) has no sharp edges left — four of the eight real anti-patterns above came directly from genuine MLflow behavior (skops, Logged Models, deprecated stages, the serving endpoint's raw error format), not from mistakes in this course's own code.
  • Fixing an anti-pattern once and assuming it can't recur — Anti-pattern 6 is exactly the kind of bug that reappears anywhere a value exists in two places instead of one real shared source.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
This capstone is not new logic anywhere — every real piece was already built and verified independently across this level and Level 3: monitoring without ground truth's proxy signals, alerting's thresholds, retraining triggers's automated kickoff, and Level 3's champion-vs-challenger gate. What this capstone verifies is that they genuinely compose correctly when run as one real, continuous loop with no human step in between — the same real kind of composition check Level 3, Lesson 10's capstone needed, now one level up, spanning detection through response instead of just response alone.

The real, complete MLOps loop this course has been building toward the whole time is exactly this: a model in production, watched by checks that don't need to wait for labels, wired to a response that doesn't need a human to notice and act, landing on a real, independently verifiable final state — whether that state is a genuinely new champion or, as in this specific real run, a correctly unchanged one.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating "the loop ran" as the same as "the loop worked" — this capstone's real final step independently re-queried the champion alias rather than trusting the retraining pipeline's own printed claims, the same discipline Level 2, Lesson 9 established for verifying a rollback actually took effect.
  • Assuming a complete MLOps loop always ends in a new deployment — this real run's correct outcome was no change, because the automated retrain, evaluated fairly, didn't beat what was already live; a loop that always deploys regardless of comparison isn't automation, it's an unconditional override.
  • Building each piece of a loop like this in isolation and never running the whole thing together — every individual piece here was already tested on its own; only running the full, real, chained loop could have confirmed detection genuinely reaches response, and response genuinely reaches a verified outcome.
